stories.headline: Five economic challenges facing Brazil's re-elected President Lula
stories.deck: Lula plans a new round of debt relief, this time through discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks, plus tax ⁠debt forgiveness for some small business owners
stories.bodyText:
Brazil's economy has beaten expectations in recent years, but mounting debt and entrenched structural problems could complicate leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's fourth term, which begins in January.
Here are the five main economic challenges he faces:
Soaring debt
Brazil’s public debt has surged more than 10 percentage points during Mr. Lula’s current term to over 82% of GDP, driving up borrowing costs.
The root cause is years of rising mandatory spending, leaving under 8% of the federal budget adjustable.
Mr. Lula has sent mixed fiscal signals, at times dismissing debt worries as “nonsense” while arguing that strong economic growth would fix the problem.
His team has pledged to keep the government's current budget rules, which cap spending growth and set primary balance targets — revenues minus expenditures, excluding interest payments on public debt — and hinted at tightening them.
Hitting those targets will be harder given Mr. Lula’s promise to raise the minimum wage faster than inflation, which also lifts pension costs, after already raising welfare benefits and promising new spending.
High interest rates and sticky inflation
Even with interest rates at 13.75%, Brazil’s annual inflation of 4.6% remains above the central bank's tolerance range of 1.5% to 4.5%.
The central bank delivered its fifth straight rate cut last month on growing signs of an economic slowdown, but markets expect inflation to remain above the official 3% target until as late as 2029.
Mr. Lula’s platform promises lower interest rates through fiscal discipline that spares social programs, but most economists say rates will only fall faster if Brazil cuts spending, and it’s unclear how he will square the two.
Debt-laden households and businesses
A record nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million businesses are behind on debt payments, according to credit bureau Serasa, as high interest rates bite.
That has fueled public dissatisfaction despite strong indicators such as record-low unemployment and wage growth outpacing inflation.
Mr. Lula plans a new round of debt relief, this time through discounted purchases of distressed household loans from banks, plus tax debt forgiveness for some small business owners. Analysts say such measures offer only temporary relief.
The government has also discussed with the central bank ways to rein in heavy use of easy but expensive credit, such as credit cards and unsecured consumer loans, though it has not detailed any proposals.
Scarce political capital for reforms
Mr. Lula will likely struggle to push his economic agenda through Congress after voters elected the most conservative legislature since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s.
Although he defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s (October 25, 2026) runoff, Mr. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies are set to control both chambers.
Mr. Lula’s aides have signalled that he will keep pushing to curtail tax breaks, but lawmakers have repeatedly resisted measures that raise the effective tax burden.
During his current term, Mr. Lula has struggled to name nominees and win Senate approval for them at key institutions, including the Supreme Court, central bank, securities regulator, and antitrust watchdog, and that is likely to be even more difficult ahead with the rightward shift of Congress.
Tax reform uncertainties
Mr. Lula won congressional approval in 2023 for a sweeping overhaul of Brazil’s consumption taxes, and a new value-added tax is set to take effect in January.
With under three months to go, the government has still not disclosed the effective rate, which independent analysts estimate will be around 28%.
Fearing a backlash during the campaign, the administration has also held off on sending Congress a bill to regulate a new tax on products considered harmful to health or the environment, such as cigarettes and alcohol.
That delay could push back revenue from the tax and has fuelled criticism of the government’s handling of tax policy.

stories.headline: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva | The democratic leftist
stories.deck: Former two-time President Lula, who has promised a new form of welfarism with ecological and infrastructure spending, defeated Brazil’s far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro in the Presidential elections
stories.bodyText:
Brazil’s former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, mononymously called Lula, on October 30 defeated incumbent Jair Bolsonaro marking a comeback and the end of a decade-long right wing rule.
On first glance, this should not be a surprise — Mr. Bolsonaro, a far-right politician, presided over a disastrous COVID-19 pandemic response in the country with nearly 700,000 registered deaths and an economy that is slowly bouncing back but is still ravaged by high inflation (as high as 11% recently). The Bolsonaro regime consistently downplayed the threat of the virus and was lax in implementing vaccination and lockdown strategies to combat the pandemic. To shore up his sagging popularity, the regime resuscitated a cash transfer scheme to the poor to tamp down the effects of high inflation, but has also increased the government’s gross debt to GDP ratio to a high 90%. Mr. Bolsonaro clearly does not enjoy the benefits of being an outsider to the establishment as he did in the 2018 elections. He has also got to reckon with the candidacy of Brazil’s most well known politician, Lula.
A former union leader who has come from humble origins, Lula served two terms as the head of State between 2003 and 2010, before demitting office to his successor Dilma Rousseff of the Workers’ Party (PT) that he helped found in 1980. As President, Lula led his country through a period of economic growth and utilised a period of high commodity prices in the international market to subsidise programmes such as Bolsa Familia that instituted conditional cash transfers for the poor and lifted an estimated 20 million people out of extreme poverty. Lula’s two-terms coincided with the pink tide — the rise of left-wing regimes in Latin America — and he served as one of the key leaders of initiatives for intra-continental cooperation besides a promoter of multilateral international organisations such as BRICS. By the time he demitted power, Lula’s personal popularity and that of his regime’s philosophy, Lulismo, remained high in Brazil.
Lula’s rule, however, was qualitatively different from the more radical socialist-oriented regimes in Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia. While his working class origins and leadership of a strong trade union in the late 1970s during the military dictatorship in Brazil firmly put him in the Left, his government utilised policies of conciliation and negotiation to advance welfare, and did not quite disturb the hold of the traditional Brazilian elite over institutions of power.
Talk with the elite
The 2000s saw the participation of more Brazilians in the polity and a greater democratisation but the PT’s strategy of negotiating with the elite in Brazil’s Congress and other institutions ensured that the corruption in the highest circles in the country remained intact, affecting even Lula’s party.
The controversial Car Wash scandal, which revealed systematic corruption in the way contracts were awarded by executives of the state-owned petroleum company Petrobras and implicated several politicians, administrators and businessmen, led to the fall of the Dilma Rousseff presidency by impeachment in 2014. Even if Ms. Rousseff was not directly implicated in the scandal, it resulted in the decline in popularity for the PT. Lula himself was arrested, convicted and was barred from participating in the 2018 presidential elections, but was released in 2019 after documents leaked by journalist Glenn Greenwald pointed to collusion by Judge Sergio Moro with the prosecution. Brazil’s Supreme Court ruled in March 2021 that justice was biased against him, resulting in the cases against him being annulled and allowing him to run for President again.
Tackling authoritarianism is not new to Lula, though. In a book that came out in 2020, author John D. French writes about how Lula rose from humble origins to become a machinist in the fast industrialising Sao Paulo region and later, a popular working class leader by mobilising industrial workers in massive strikes during the dictatorship in the late 1970s. Lula’s style has always been to utilise dialogue with political opponents without giving up on an ability to “stand up and fight, when needed .. [through] an additive and transformative politics of cunning executed by creating spaces of convergence through difference”. Lula emerged as one of the key politicians in the newly democratic Brazil of the late 1980s after having cut his teeth as a working class leader and a leader of a national trade union confederation. His style of leadership and an ability to speak to Brazil’s poor through a unique “vernacular discourse” was intact both as a trade unionist and a popular politician and the leader of the PT.
Once in power, he continued to use the strategy of dialogue but moderated the ideological impulses of the PT even as he embarked upon welfare programmes that benefited the party’s core base. Yet, the PT and Lula’s critics in the left spectrum in Brazil argue that the party’s strategy to utilise a policy of conciliation and negotiation with the traditional elite allowed it to pursue reforms without blowback but it also helped the fortunes of the richer sections in Brazil — particularly those in the agro-economy sector. They argue that this also paved the way for the parliamentary “coup” from the Right that led to the impeachment of Ms. Rousseff besides the corruption cases giving a fillip to the rise of the far-right led by Mr. Bolsonaro.
Mr. Bolsonaro has never hidden his support for the erstwhile military dictatorship and has also suggested, in Donald Trump-like fashion — to whom his personality and politics are likened to —, that a loss in the elections would only mean electoral fraud, suggesting to his supporters that he will not accept defeat. There is now fear among some Brazilians that Mr. Bolsonaro and his supporters might stage an insurrection in the likelihood of an electoral defeat.
Social liberalism
Lula’s triumphs against Mr. Bolsonaro is a victory for political decency and social liberalism over far-right populism and crass political discourse in Latin America’s largest country. Lula has promised that if he comes to power, he would implement new welfare, ecological and infrastructure spending schemes based on Keynesianism. But it would be a struggle for him to negotiate with a truculent and more powerful Brazilian Congress than during the 2000s.

stories.headline: Crude prices fall from six-month highs; WTI stands at $101 per barrel, Brent costs $115
stories.deck: Oil prices experienced a decline of over 1% after hitting six-month peaks, primarily due to geopolitical unrest in Saudi Arabia. Currently, Brent crude fluctuates around $115 per barrel, and WTI at $101.5 per barrel. The threat to energy exports and infrastructure from Houthi attacks raises alarm, while the Federal Reserve meeting looms, potentially addressing inflation amid climbing energy…
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices fell over 1% on Monday after surging to near six-month highs late last week. Despite the decline, prices remained elevated, with Brent crude hovering near $115 per barrel as continued attacks on Saudi Arabia kept concerns over global oil supplies alive.
The US Federal Reserve's upcoming policy decision is another factor investors will watch as crude enters a potentially volatile week.
WTI crude fell 1.71%, or $1.77, to $101.5 per barrel, while Brent crude declined 1.41%, or $1.65, to $115.1 per barrel.
The decline followed a sharp rise on Friday, when prices settled nearly $3 higher after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised concerns about energy supplies. Brent recorded a 6% gain for the week, while WTI advanced 2.3%, taking prices close to six-month highs.
The security situation remained tense over the weekend. The Houthis said they had attacked a Saudi airport and oil facilities on Saturday, while Saudi Arabia reported intercepting additional missiles and drones on Sunday. The country's main airport resumed partial operations the same day, following damage from an earlier round of Houthi attacks. The militant group has vowed to continue targeting the facility.
Strait of Hormuz remains a key concern
Developments around the Strait of Hormuz and the security of energy infrastructure are expected to influence crude prices in the coming days. Brent has already crossed $117 per barrel, and analysts said any disruption to energy facilities or shipping through the strait could push global prices towards $120 per barrel. A credible move towards de-escalation, however, could lead to a sharp correction.
"The near-term bias remains bullish but highly headline-driven; traders should avoid chasing sharp rallies and monitor geopolitical developments, Fed guidance and weekly inventory data for directional confirmation," said Ajit Mishra, SVP - Research at Religare Broking.
The latest price rally has been driven by escalating US-Iran tensions, fears of renewed military action, attacks on Saudi infrastructure and threats to important shipping routes, Mishra said. These developments have sustained the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices.
Navneet Damani, head of research - commodities at Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd, said, "The rally gathered pace as attention returned to escalating attacks around the Hormuz and Saudi Arabia, reviving concerns over energy infrastructure and export security."
Further uncertainty has emerged from reports that the US and Israel had prepared plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure, including nuclear facilities near Natanz, after the US mid-term elections on November 3. Iran warned of repercussions if Washington and Tel Aviv launched an attack, adding to concerns in the market.
Supply measures fail to reverse the rally
Efforts to ease supply concerns have so far done little to bring prices down. The International Energy Agency has indicated its readiness to release more strategic stocks, while the G7's additional 100 million barrels largely involves accelerating an existing release programme. The first Russian diesel cargo bound for the US has also failed to reverse the upward trend.
According to Damani, market participants are now looking for evidence that these measures will translate into meaningful additional supplies, rather than responding to announcements alone.
"Although crude flows through Hormuz have shown some recovery, elevated freight costs, constrained regional shipments and persistent security threats continue to undermine export reliability. With physical supply yet to normalise, the risk premium remains elevated, and the balance of risks continues to favour the upside, though credible progress towards de-escalation could still trigger sharp profit-taking," Damani added.
The market will also track weekly US inventory estimates from the American Petroleum Institute and the US Energy Information Administration, alongside Cushing crude inventories. These figures could offer further direction as traders assess the state of supply.

stories.headline: Muslim World League condemns Houthi missile attacks targeting Mecca, Medina
stories.bodyText: Dubai: The Muslim World League on Sunday condemned what it described as Houthi missile attacks targeting Saudi Arabia's Makkah and Madinah regions, saying they violated the sanctity of Islam's holy sites. . Saudi Civil Defense said two ballistic missiles launched towards the two regions were intercepted on Saturday, with debris falling in Wadi Al-Mughammas in Makkah, Al-Nuzha neighbourhood in Jeddah, Wadi Jalil in Taif and Masturah Centre in Rabigh. The authorities said established procedures for such incidents had been carried out but did not provide information on casualties. . The Houthis, however, have denied targeting Makkah and Madinah, saying their operations were directed at oil facilities and military sites. . In its statement, Muslim World League Secretary-General Mohammed bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa described the attacks as a "dangerous provocation" of the sentiments of more than two billion Muslims. .Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif. The League said the attacks constituted "a betrayal of religion and Muslims" and reaffirmed its "full solidarity" with Saudi Arabia in measures to deter further attacks and safeguard holy sites and civilians. . The Muslim World League is an international Islamic organisation headquartered in Makkah. Established in 1962, it says its mission is to explain Islam's teachings and promote friendship and understanding among peoples. . Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have intensified in recent weeks, with the group claiming attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and military sites. Saudi authorities have reported intercepting missiles and drones targeting the kingdom. . The latest developments come amid wider tensions over Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key international shipping route.

briefs.headline: Brazil's Lula da Silva defies odds to clinch poll victory against Flavio Bolsonaro
briefs.deck: According to official results, he won 51.75% of the votes to 48.25% for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls
briefs.bodyText:
Brazil's leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday (October 25, 2026) as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round.
The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday (October 27), defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term at the helm of Latin America's largest country.
According to official results, he won 51.75% of the votes to 48.25% for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.
With Mr. Lula's victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday's (October 25) vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Mr. Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension.
"Either we win. Or we win. Consider yourself warned," pro-Bolsonaro lawmaker Nikolas Ferreira wrote on X as the votes streamed in.
The bitter campaign laid bare the deep divisions in the country of over 200 million people.
"It's a disgrace. We've never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they've come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours," said Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasilia.
Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Mr. Lula said it was "more than fair...everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected."
Lula rises from the ashes, again
Mr. Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, was blindsided after his first-round defeat to Mr. Bolsonaro.
The left swung into action with massive rallies declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro," where protesters recalled the former president's chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs.
Mr. Lula also revamped his social media strategy, taking video selfies and even bought his first cellphone, while supporters carried out a feverish campaign to change the minds of family, friends and neighbours, and encourage them to vote after high levels of abstention.
His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers.
Mr. Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.
The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term, he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity.
Mr. Lula's social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign.
"Brazil needs more time with Lula, primarily because the country is on the verge of falling into the clutches of fascism," Maria Fernanda Elisbao, a 21-year-old editorial assistant, told AFP.
A tricky term ahead
Mr. Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation voting against him and desperate for change.
"We're in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question," said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.
Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Mr. Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.
He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as President from 2003 to 2010.
Mr. Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.
His options are also constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow.
He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant insecurity in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighbourhoods.
The President's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Mr. Trump's United States.
Voters must "choose a country where the flag is respected," he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to "govern with the American flag."

briefs.headline: A physicist who took atoms near absolute zero, and physics further
briefs.deck: Claude Cohen-Tannoudji had many connections with India, including acknowledging the work of a little-known scientist who had died three decades before Cohen-Tannoudji won the Nobel Prize
briefs.bodyText:
The French physicist Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, who helped develop techniques to cool atoms to barely above absolute zero using laser light, passed away on October 22, aged 93. His work revolutionised physics by giving scientists a way to manipulate atoms and probe their quantum properties, work for which he won a piece of the physics Nobel Prize in 1997.
As it happens, Cohen-Tannoudji also had many connections with physics in India, including acknowledging the work of a little-known — even in India — physicist who had died three decades before the prize was awarded.
Cohen-Tannoudji was born in French Algeria in 1933. He moved to Paris when he was 20 to study mathematics, before lectures by the physicist Alfred Kastler convinced him he should be studying physics instead. He soon joined a group led by Kastler and Jean Brossel in 1955 and then spent most of his career at the institution since called the Laboratoire Kastler Brossel.
Sisyphus cooling
Conventionally, lasers are good at delivering energy to objects, so the idea of using them to cool atoms down can seem counterintuitive. The key detail is that laser light also has momentum.
In one technique called Doppler cooling, scientists shine laser beams at atoms from different directions. The lasers are configured such that an atom moving towards one laser beam is more likely to absorb photons from that source than from the beams on other sides. When the atom has absorbed a photon, its own energy briefly rises before falling again as the atom spits the photon back out.
Here is the catch: the atom always absorbs photons in one direction but spits it out in random directions. So the kick provided by the exiting photon is cancelled by the kicks the atom is getting in multiple directions — whereas the reverse-kick happens in only one direction: in the direction of that one laser beam. So as the atom repeatedly absorbs and emits photons, its average kinetic energy, and therefore its temperature, drops.
Clever though it was, Doppler cooling had a lower limit: as the atom cooled, the lasers became less effective at slowing it further because they could no longer distinguish the direction of motion as easily. In 1988, the U.S. physicist William Phillips led a team that produced atoms colder than the Doppler cooling limit — and Cohen-Tannoudji and his peers, but especially Jean Dalibard, explained how this was possible. It had to do with the polarisation of light and the energy levels of the electrons in the target atoms.
Their explanation proved important because it led to a new technique called Sisyphus cooling, named for the doomed figure in Greek mythology who had to keep rolling a boulder uphill only for it to roll down again. Here, an atom’s kinetic energy is repeatedly converted to potential energy, which is ‘pumped out’ using a technique similar to Doppler cooling.
The name of the technique comes from a different way to visualise the atom’s experience, so to speak. Lasers are used to create a space where the atom, in motion, is forced to move from a part where it has lower potential energy to where it has more. The same thing happens when you climb a staircase: as you go from the ground floor to the first floor, you expend kinetic energy as you move but your body also accumulates more potential energy.
Once the atom is at the ‘top’, a process called an optical pump cools it down to have less energy than when it was on the ground floor. Then it is forced to climb another set of stairs. This way, repeatedly, the atom can be cooled to extremely low temperatures.
Cohen-Tannoudji’s group developed methods to cool atoms to a few nanokelvins — billionths of a degree above absolute zero — paving the way for advanced atomic clocks and atom interferometers.
Remembering Pancharatnam
In 1994, Cohen-Tannoudji contributed a three-page essay for a special issue of the Indian journal Current Science commemorating physicist S. Pancharatnam, who had worked with C.V. Raman in Bangalore (now Bengaluru) and later with George William Series in Britain. Unfortunately, Pancharatnam passed away in 1969, when he was only 35.
Pancharatnam did most of his work before tunable lasers became widely available, and in the same areas as Cohen-Tannoudji. In his article, Cohen-Tannoudji recalled Pancharatnam’s “series of beautiful papers” on optical pumping and remarked that recent developments in the field would have pleased him. He also acknowledged that some of the theoretical foundations of (then) contemporary laser cooling techniques had been considered well before the experimental proof could be devised.
The same issue of Current Science also featured an essay by the British physicist Michael Berry, who recalled visiting Bangalore in 1987 and discussing the work of Pancharatnam with Sivaraj Ramaseshan, which he said helped him appreciate the connection with Pancharatnam’s previous work and Berry’s own in the 1980s.
Cohen-Tannoudji visited Bangalore again in early 1999, where he participated in an Indo-French workshop at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics. He also visited the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai on the same trip, where he delivered the first Homi J. Bhabha Lecture, followed by a lecture in New Delhi.
He also co-authored a 2001 paper in Physical Review Letters with C.S. Unnikrishnan that reported an unusual phase of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate in a thin gas of helium — a significant achievement in atomic physics.
Cohen-Tannoudji was widely regarded as a generous figure in a profession that more than rarely featured fierce competition, and competitive personalities. Alain Aspect, who won a share of the physics Nobel Prize in 2022, has said that while some senior physicists considered Aspect’s early work (on experimentally testing the Bell’s inequalities) to be a waste of time, Cohen-Tannoudji was encouraging and helped Aspect be taken seriously.
In one 2015 interview to Weizmann Direct, a publication of the Weizmann Institute in Israel, Cohen-Tannoudji recalled organising meetings bringing Israeli and Arab, including Palestinian, scientists together for week-long discussions. He signed a letter in 2021 calling for the release of doctor and human rights activist Binayak Sen. A tributary statement from the Laboratoire Kastler Brossel after his passing also recalled his willingness to discuss ideas with anyone who approached him.

briefs.headline: BJP uses 'money, intimidation' to influence people, Mamata Banerjee claims
Magnitude 5.2 earthquake strikes Afghanistan's Hindu Kush region
'Congress is like mafia': BJP slams Kharge's 'Modi ka baap' remark
briefs.bodyText: New Delhi: Hitting out at Mallikarjun Kharge for his disparaging "personal" remarks against Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the BJP on Sunday said the Congress chief is using language "associated with thugs and hooligans", reflecting the "ideological bankruptcy" of his party that appears more like a "mafia gang". . The ruling party also announced that it will hold nationwide protests on Monday against the Congress president's "insulting, indecent and offensive" remarks. . The BJP's strong reaction followed Kharge's outburst during a function on the 139th birth anniversary of Bihar's first chief minister, Shrikrishna Singh, in Patna, where he said that the Congress will send those involved in carrying out alleged irregularities in the SIR process to jail. . "Modi ka baap bhi jayega, baap bhi jayega ( Even Modi's father would go)," Kharge retorted from the dais, after a member of the audience interrupted the Congress chief's speech and shouted, "As long as there is no rebellion, Modi won't go anywhere." . BJP chief Nitin Nabin said the people of the country are watching this "indecent politics very closely and will give it a befitting reply in due time". . "The kind of indecent and unparliamentary language used today in Patna by Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge towards the country's honourable Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi ji reflects the Congress party's ideological bankruptcy," Nabin said on X. . He said political opposition too should have some dignity. "But dragging the departed family members into speeches from public platforms has now become the real 'culture' of Rahul Gandhi and the entire opposition," Nabin said. . "The language that was once associated with thugs and hooligans is now being used by the Congress President himself... Their entire style of functioning has turned into that of a mafia. This isn't a political party anymore -- it seems more like a mafia gang," the BJP said on its X handle. .As long as RSS ideology persists, there will be no peace in India: Mallikarjun Kharge. The BJP's allies LJP and JD(U) also condemned Kharge's remarks. . Home Minister Amit Shah said that Kharge has today "torn apart all norms of decorum by making an indecent remark about Modi ji's father in Patna". . "This is not the first time that the Congress party has used abusive language against Modi ji or his family. At times, they have hurled insults at his revered mother, at times called him 'merchant of death,' and at times mocked his poverty by calling him 'chaiwala.' . "People of the country will surely deliver their response to such petty politics through democratic means," he added. . Nadda said the opposition's "panic", stemming from Modi's rising popularity at home and abroad, and the people's unwavering trust in him are now plainly evident in its language and conduct. And today this frustration was visible," he told reporters here. . BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad said Kharge's remarks against PM Modi were "shameful, undignified and petty", and demanded that both Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi apologise. . "We strongly condemn this (Kharge's remarks). People of the country are watching all of this and will give a fitting reply, as seen in the recent by-elections and municipal polls. The Congress party will be wiped out everywhere," Prasad told reporters. . The BJP said it will hold protests against Kharge's remarks across the country on Monday. . briefs.headline: Hindutva reading builds on colonial interpretations of Indian history: Romila Thapar
briefs.deck: Had greater attention been paid to physical evidence such as inscriptions, Indian history may have been interpreted differently, says the historian
briefs.bodyText:
Historian Romila Thapar, 96, on Sunday (October 25, 2026) argued that colonial historians fundamentally shaped the way Indian history came to be understood, reducing complex social and political processes to simplified religious narratives that continue to influence historical interpretations today and propagate the Hindutva reading of Indian history.
Delivering the Second Sitaram Yechury Memorial Lecture on the theme, “Historiography and Early Indian History”, Ms. Thapar said the subject stemmed from a brief conversation she once had with the late CPI(M) leader.
Reflecting on her career as a historian of ancient India, Ms. Thapar said she had expected a quiet academic life when she entered the profession. “History is playing a public role, which it never did in the past,” she said, noting the growing public contestation over interpretations of the past.
Tracing the origins of many prevailing ideas about Indian history, Ms. Thapar said colonial scholars viewed India through the framework of “Oriental despotism”, portraying Asian societies as static and unchanging and governed by despotic rulers. She argued that the tendency to read Indian history primarily through a religious lens was also inherited from colonial scholarship.
Had greater attention been paid to physical evidence such as inscriptions, Indian history might have been interpreted differently, she said. Referring to the period after the Gupta era, Ms. Thapar noted the abundance of inscriptions documenting governance practices, caste relations and various aspects of social life, providing a richer understanding of the past than reliance on religious texts alone.
‘Own invention’
“Those writing the history of the colony were writing their own invention,” she said, pointing to British historian James Mill, whom she credited with advancing the idea of India as divided into Hindu and Muslim nations permanently hostile to each other.
Ms. Thapar said colonial historians oversimplified a wide range of social and political conflicts by presenting them as manifestations of religious antagonism. Such accounts created “mono-causal” explanations that ignored other factors.
Citing the Battle of Haldighati, she said the conflict was essentially a territorial contest. She noted that Rana Pratap’s forces included Afghan soldiers, while the Mughal army was led by a Rajput commander. Yet, the battle was now frequently presented as a defining confrontation between a Hindu ruler and a Muslim invader.
Ms. Thapar also criticised Mill’s periodisation of Indian history into the “Hindu”, “Muslim” and “British” periods, arguing that such categorisations imposed simplistic divisions on a far more complex historical experience.
In this context, she said the decolonisation of history should depend on the new evidence available, thanks to the advances made in archeology and genetic, instead of building further on the colonial reading of history emphasising on religious fractures.
The Hindutva reading of Indian history was “single and fixed”, she said, which did not take into account the multiplicity within the Hinduism itself, citing the example of Vishnu’s avatar Jagannath in Odisha and Vithal in Maharashtra being two distinct entities. “In this interpretation, the purpose of history is not to explain what happened in the past, but instead to construct statements of contemporary political views. These statements deny the centrality of secularism and democracy as the essential component of the new nation,” she said.

stories.headline: Pulakeshinagar IED blast case cracked, personal rivalry behind the plot
stories.deck: The Bengaluru police have cracked the case of the recent blast at an under-construction building on Jeremiah Road, injuring two, and arrested a 27-year-old bakery salesman, who allegedly conspired with two childhood friends to murder his uncle by assembling an improvised explosive device (IED) concealed inside a parcel
stories.bodyText:
The Bengaluru police have cracked the case of the recent blast at an under-construction building on Jeremiah Road, injuring two, and arrested a 27-year-old bakery salesman, who allegedly conspired with two childhood friends to murder his uncle by assembling an improvised explosive device (IED) concealed inside a parcel.
According to the police, the prime accused held a grudge against his uncle, Allauddin M., over property and financial disputes, as well as a personal issue involving the breakdown of his sister’s marriage.
The incident occurred on October 20 when workers were at the building. A loud explosion was heard on the fifth floor, and an investigation revealed that an IED concealed inside a torch had exploded.
The IED was assembled in Raichur by one of the conspirators, who learned from YouTube. Material obtained from firecrackers was used as the explosive material in the IED, rigged inside a battery using an electrical circuit and pellets.
Investigators said the accused had prepared a parcel containing the device and left it at a petty shop near the building where Allauddin was working. The accused allegedly contacted him over the phone and pressured him to open the parcel.
Allauddin, who was having lunch, asked his colleague to open it and the device exploded when the parcel was opened. Allauddin and his colleague, Suraj Kumar, a security guard from Uttar Pradesh, sustained severe injuries.
The case had led to speculations of terrorism owing to the involvement of an IED, even as sleuths from the National Investigation Agency (NIA) also joined the probe.
Home Minister Priyank Kharge had appealed to not give into rumours, even as the Bengaluru City Police launched a massive operation to crack the case. Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said around 1,200 personnel had worked in different teams during the investigation and announced a ₹3 Lakh reward for those who cracked the case.

stories.headline: Over 61,000 Form-7 applications filed by election officials in Karnataka, none cites reason
stories.deck: Officials say they were instructed to file Form-7 applications for shifted, duplicate, underage, deceased and non-citizen voters, but auto-generated forms left the reason blank
stories.bodyText:
At least 61,059 Form-7 applications seeking the deletion of names from Karnataka’s electoral rolls were filed by election officials themselves, with not a single application mentioning a reason for the deletion, a mandatory requirement under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs), listed as the objectors in these applications, said the system “auto-generated” the forms with their digital signatures when voters could not be reached during hearings on notices issued for no mapping or logical discrepancies, and the voters were therefore marked as “ineligible”.
This meant the same election machinery was raising objections to voters’ names and deciding on whether they should remain on the rolls. Under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 an objection that is not filed in the prescribed manner, including stating the reason, is liable to be rejected.
The officials said they had been instructed to file Form-7 applications if a voter had shifted, had a duplicate entry elsewhere, was underage, had died, or was not an Indian citizen. But as the forms were auto-generated, the reason for seeking deletion was left blank.
With no reason recorded, neither the voter nor anyone examining the electoral roll can establish why a particular name was marked for deletion or verify whether the removal was justified.
Moreover, these categories of voters (ASDDO or Absent, Shifted, Duplicate, Dead and Others) had already been checked during the enumeration phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which led to more than 1.07 crore names being deleted from Karnataka’s draft electoral roll. Most deletions were on the grounds of voters having permanently shifted, followed by those marked as absent.
Rise after objections window
The number of Form-7 applications filed by election officials rose sharply after the claims and objections period ended on September 23, 2026. Between August 24 and September 23, only 192 such applications were received. More than 60,800 were filed after the claims and objections period, between September 24 and October 22.
The filing continued at an exceptionally high rate even as the disposal deadline approached. On October 22, the last day for disposing of claims and objections, election officials filed 10,105 Form-7 applications. Another 10,314 were filed on the previous day, October 21. On October 17 and 19, officials filed 11,132 and 11,760 applications, respectively.
Already deleted
To examine the pattern, The Hindu obtained the EPIC numbers of several voters against whom election officials had filed Form-7 applications and cross-checked their details on the Election Commission of India (ECI) portal. In all the cases checked, the names had already been deleted from the electoral roll, including those against whom applications had been filed after September 23.
This is at odds with Rule 17 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, which states that any claim or objection not lodged within the prescribed period or in the prescribed form and manner “shall be rejected by the registration officer”. It also remains unclear whether hearing notices or orders, which are mandatory before deletion, were issued in these cases, or on what grounds the names were deleted, as the relevant details had been left blank.
In the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike South district, where election officials filed the highest number of Form-7 applications, applications filed by officials outnumbered those filed by voters or third parties. Of the 17,491 applications in the district, 10,374 were filed by officials. In the Bommanahalli Assembly constituency alone, officials filed 4,095 of the 5,757 applications received.
The pattern of EROs and AEROs filing more Form-7 applications than voters or third parties was seen in at least 26 Assembly constituencies.
Karnataka’s final electoral roll is scheduled to be published on October 27. Only claims and objections received by September 23 were to be considered for the final roll. Applications filed after the deadline were to be considered only for a supplementary roll after the SIR. However, The Hindu’s sample checks found that the names of voters cited in applications filed even after the deadline had already been deleted from the roll.
It is also pertinent to note that the actual number could be higher as the number of Form-7 applications available in the consolidated Form-10 records on the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) website has consistently been lower than the figures cited in statements issued by the Chief Electoral Officer of Karnataka. The Hindu had highlighted this discrepancy in an earlier report.
Between September 24 and October 22, the CEO’s office reported 1,70,442 Form-7 applications. However, only 1,56,634 applications were available in the consolidated Form-10 records on the ECI website, leaving a gap of 13,808 applications.

stories.headline: Damaged curd packet: Bengaluru woman loses Rs 98k in fake refund scam
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A damaged packet of curd led to cyber fraud of Rs 98,000 after a 56-year-old homemaker tried to seek a refund for the product ordered through the quick-commerce platform Blinkit.
According to a complaint filed by 
Soundarya
 (name changed), a resident of an apartment on Palace Cross Road in Vasanth Nagar, she had ordered a packet of curd online on Oct 17. When it was delivered, it was in a damaged condition, the woman stated. She complained to the delivery agent, who asked her to contact customer care.
She searched online and called a number she found on the internet. The person who answered the call promised a refund and asked her to follow a few instructions. He sent a link to her on WhatsApp and instructed her to upload a photograph of the damaged packet. After she submitted the photo, another fraudster called her, claiming that a refund would be processed and asking her to check her digital payment account.
However, when she opened the account and entered her password to check the balance, the app disappeared from the screen, she said. Soon, Rs 98,000 was deducted from her bank account, she added.
Realising that she had been cheated, she approached police and sought action. Central Cyber Crime police registered a case and are investigating.

stories.headline: Home-alone woman, 70, found murdered in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A 70-year-old woman who lived alone at Hosa Guddadahalli on Mysuru Road was found murdered at her home Saturday evening.
Byatarayanapura police are investigating whether Venkatlakshmamma was killed for her valuables or out of enmity by someone known to her.
It is suspected that the incident occurred on the afternoon of Oct 23, when assailants entered her house on C Cross, 1st Main Road, and attacked her before escaping.
The crime came to light after neighbours noticed that Venkatlakshmamma had not stepped out of her house for almost 24 hours. When they checked on her, they found her dead with injuries to her head.
Venkatlakshmamma owned four houses, and she lived alone in one of them, while one Lekhith rented another. The remaining two houses were vacant. Her only daughter had died of an illness around two years ago, and her husband had passed away a few years ago.
According to a complaint filed by Lekhith (21), he received information that the woman had collapsed inside her house. He said he found her lying in a pool of blood. He called the emergency helpline 112. Byatarayanapura police visited the spot and collected evidence.
Venkatlakshmamma would always keep the compound gates and the door of her house locked as hardly anyone visited her. During his occasional visits, Lekhith would call her on her mobile phone to ask her to open the gates. He also helped her obtain medication for her diabetes once a month. Venkatlakshmamma owned properties in a nearby area too.
Deputy commissioner of police (west) Yathish N said the reason for the murder would be ascertained only after the accused were apprehended. Special teams have been formed to nab the suspects, police said.

briefs.headline: Karnataka Congress on image revival mode, activates its poll strategists

Karnataka Congress

Senior party functionaries told TOI that Sunil Kanagolu, the party’s key strategist and chief adviser to chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
, has set up shop and is building a team in Karnataka. They are expected to launch an extensive campaign as early as Jan 2027.
Kanagolu, along with Thiruvallur (Tamil Nadu) Congress MP Sasikant Senthil, a former IAS officer, played a key role in the party’s 2023 victory. Two other agencies believed to be close to Shivakumar have also reportedly been activated to prepare for a challenge from the BJP-JD(S) NDA alliance.
The early mobilisation comes as the govt faces mounting criticism over financial concerns, the sting operation controversy and prolonged internal factionalism, which have dented its image and affected cadre morale. Party sources say the strategists would help improve the govt’s image and reshape the political narrative.
A recent private survey projected Congress winning 79 seats in 2028, against 145 for the BJP-JD(S) alliance if elections were held under the prevailing circumstances.
However, deputy CM G Parameshwara said the party was not worried about current projections and that there is enough time to prepare.
“We will strive to work harder for the welfare of the people. What is the point of talking about today’s situation?” said Parameshwara.
Senior Congress legislators, meanwhile, stressed the need to strengthen the party’s organisational structure before the strategists begin work.
“For them to operate, the party needs to have cadre strength. We are still in the process of appointing district Congress committee (DCC) presidents and other office-bearers. Only after we have the right apparatus in place can the strategists start working,” said a legislator.

briefs.headline: Congress takes ‘Vote bachao, desh bachao’ to Mangaluru
briefs.deck: AICC leader Kamaleshwar Patel alleges electoral irregularities, cites Mahadevapura voter entries
briefs.bodyText:
Mangaluru: 
Congress
 has stepped up its district-level ‘Vote bachao, desh bachao’ campaign in Mangaluru, with AICC working committee member Kamaleshwar Patel alleging electoral irregularities and deletion of voters’ names from electoral rolls.
Patel told reporters Sunday that the campaign would mobilise citizens to protect their constitutional rights.
“The ongoing incidents of vote theft are a direct assault on our democracy,” he said.
Patel said, “In Karnataka’s Mahadevapura assembly constituency alone, an analysis of 10,00,500 voter entries exposed 11,956 duplicate names, 40,009 unauthentic addresses, and 10,452 registrations sharing a single address.”
Patel also cited figures from recent elections, alleging that continuous scrutiny through SIR mechanisms had led to the removal of 1,30,30,000 votes across the country.
MLC Manjunath Bhandary said the campaign was necessary to protect voters’ democratic rights. “We cannot remain silent while the democratic voices of our people are being systematically suppressed, and this campaign ensures every legitimate vote remains secured.”
DCC president Padmaraj R Poojary said party workers were reaching out across the district to raise awareness of alleged electoral irregularities.
Patel also alleged that Maharashtra’s voter rolls saw an unprecedented addition of 40,00,000 voters in just five months between the 2024 Lok Sabha and subsequent assembly elections, despite adult population projections showing only 3,200,000 growth over five years. Patel alleged similar massive discrepancies and suspicious duplicate entries in Haryana and West Bengal.
Launching a scathing attack on the central govt, he said, “Despite objections being raised by the other two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, against the conduct of Gyanesh Kumar, no action had been taken nor was there any response from either the 
Election Commission of India
 or the govt, as Gyanesh Kumar is completely working under the influence of home minister Amit Shah and Prime Minister Narendra Modi,” he alleged, questioning the credibility of the central govt being voted to power by means of electoral fraud.
All India Congress Committee (AICC) launched the nationwide ‘Vote bachao, desh bachao’ campaign against alleged electoral fraud and deletion of voters’ names from electoral rolls. Spearheaded by AICC president 
Mallikarjun Kharge
 and Lok Sabha opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, the campaign aims to safeguard citizens’ voting rights.
The nationwide campaign began on Oct 10 and will continue until Nov 26, with major rallies scheduled in New Delhi on Nov 1 and around Constitution Day on Nov 26. District-level awareness programmes are being held across various districts, including Mangaluru, Maharashtra, Haryana, and West Bengal.

briefs.headline: IMD forecasts rain in Bengaluru as Bay depression heads towards Andhra coast
briefs.deck: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast light to moderate rain or thundershowers, heavy at times, in Bengaluru over the next 24 hours
briefs.bodyText:
With a depression over the Bay of Bengal expected to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday, Bengaluru is likely to receive light to moderate rain or thundershowers, heavy at times, over the next 24 hours, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Sunday.
Between October 26 and 31, scattered to isolated rainfall is likely over parts of South Interior Karnataka, including Bengaluru Urban and Bengaluru Rural districts. The IMD has forecast light to moderate rain at a few places in Bengaluru Urban and Rural, Chamarajanagar and other parts of South Interior Karnataka. Mainly dry weather is likely in Ballari, Chitradurga, Davanagere, Chikkaballapura, Mandya and Vijayanagara districts.
The city is likely to remain generally cloudy, with the maximum and minimum temperatures around 27 degrees Celsius and 21 degrees Celsius, respectively. Light to moderate rain or thundershowers are also likely on Monday (October 26).
The depression is expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm over the east-central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday morning, and into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal around Tuesday morning, the weather body said.
Thereafter, it is likely to move northwestwards and intensify further into a very severe cyclonic storm, reaching the west-central Bay of Bengal near the Andhra Pradesh coast around Wednesday morning. It is very likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam by Wednesday forenoon, with maximum sustained wind speeds of 115-125 kmph.

stories.headline: GSTAT allows GST refund on cancelled air tickets
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: GST paid on cancelled airline tickets can be claimed as a refund if the airline has returned both the fare and GST to the passengers and has supporting documents to prove it, a GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) has ruled.
Ruling in the case of Singapore Airlines v/s Kochi Commissioner of CGST & CE, Kochi, Ernakulam bench of GSTAT has decided that there is “sufficient evidence” to ensure that the refund of cancelled tickets has reached the respective passengers directly and there is “no passing” of the incidence of tax.
The GSTAT directed the revenue department to process the refund claim of the airline within two weeks and make payment along with interest.
The case relates to eight GST refund claims totalling Rs 45,92,528 by Singapore Airlines for the period between Oct 2019 and March 2021. During the period, owing to Covid-19, the airline had to cancel flights and returned fares and GST to passengers. However, it could not adjust the credit notes against output tax.
The GST joint commissioner had earlier rejected the refund claims, following which the appellant approached the GSTAT. 
Setting aside the JC(A) order, GSTAT in its order dated Oct 16 said, “The appellant airline is eligible for refund of GST collected from passengers and paid by them to the GST department, but subsequently refunded the entire amount of fare, including GST, to the passengers, on account of cancellation of the flights due to the Covid-19 pandemic in terms of Hon’ble Supreme Court’s order.”
The GSTAT also concluded that the appellant has provided sufficient evidence to ensure that the refund of the cancelled tickets have reached the respective passenger. Rahul Shekhar, partner—indirect tax at Nangia Global, said the ruling is a positive development, as GST should not become a cost where a transaction is cancelled, and the tax collected is fully refunded to customers.

stories.headline: UPI and the cost of policy reversal
stories.deck: The government’s proposal to allow an MDR of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000 reverses a decade-long policy; taxing the payment rail could weaken incentives for banks and fintechs to invest in UPI while undermining its role in financial inclusion, formalisation and wider digital adoption
stories.bodyText:
The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters.
This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received.
The policy reversal
Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered.
There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury.
Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed.
There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics.
Who really pays?
First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky.
The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance.
The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth.
Cost to inclusion
Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile.
Also read| Pay wall: On a charge on UPI transactions
Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016.
Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage.
The proposal is being dressed up as a modest, targeted measure affecting only large-value transactions. But modest measures on payment rails have a way of expanding once the legal architecture exists. Section 10A, once amended, does not expire when this particular MDR proposal is shelved. The better outcome is for the government to leave the payments system alone, let UPI’s network effects keep compounding, and find its revenue elsewhere.
(Parag Waknis, Professor & Head, Economics Department, SRM University AP)

stories.headline: How India’s life insurance sector funds government expenditure
stories.deck: A significant share of life insurance premiums is reinvested in securities that finance government expenditure. While the case for deeper insurance penetration is often made in terms of household financial protection, it is equally important for sovereign fiscal stability
stories.bodyText:
When the government borrows, the question that follows is rarely asked aloud: who lends? A large part of the answer is the life insurance sector. Every year, millions of households across India pay premiums into life insurance policies. That money is reinvested, for decades, in the very securities that finance government expenditure — roads, railways, water supplies, hospitals, defence. The household protecting itself against the loss of its breadwinner is simultaneously, and unknowingly, lending to the sovereign [the Central government]. Life insurers collectively hold close to a quarter of India’s outstanding central government dated securities, based on RBI and IRDAI data — a share that has remained stable even as the total sovereign debt stock expanded by around 40 per cent in three years. This is not a number that appears in budget speeches or parliamentary debates. It is, however, a number that matters.
Patient capital in a volatile world
The stoic and resilient quality of the sector’s sovereign support is as significant as its scale. Life insurers write policies with tenures of twenty, thirty, sometimes forty years. Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market. Unlike foreign portfolio investors, whose appetite fluctuates with global risk sentiment, insurance companies buy and hold. They do not exit when oil prices rise or when a geopolitical event triggers a reassessment of emerging market exposure. Their participation is counter-cyclical by design — stable precisely when other buyers become unreliable. A steady domestic base of long-horizon holders reduces rollover risk and moderates borrowing costs across the maturity spectrum.
Life insurers buy when others sell, hold when others exit, and reinvest when others pause. That is the structural consequence of writing long-duration promises to millions of policyholders.
The heavyweight within the sector
The sector’s contribution is not evenly distributed. The Life Insurance Corporation of India carries the dominant share — a consequence of its scale, its predominantly participating product mix, and the duration of its in-force book. Its March 2025 regulatory filing with IRDAI (Form L-26) confirms that sovereign paper accounts for nearly 63 per cent of its non-linked policyholder corpus — well above the regulatory minimum, and a direct expression of what long-duration liabilities demand at scale.
LIC holds approximately 19 per cent of all outstanding central government dated securities — a figure confirmed by the RBI’s Public Debt Management Quarterly Report for FY24, the most recently published data. LIC’s IRDAI regulatory filings for March 2025 give the institutional reality in absolute terms: ₹20.2 lakh crore in central government securities alone, and ₹32.3 lakh crore in total government and government-guaranteed securities across all funds. These are not estimates. They are figures LIC files with its regulator every quarter and that any researcher can access on the IRDAI website. This makes LIC the single largest institutional holder of Indian government’s debt.
Private life insurers, with a higher proportion of unit-linked and shorter-tenure products, contribute a smaller fraction today. As they grow and deepen their traditional offerings, their sovereign allocations will follow the same structural logic.
The regulator has already recognised the systemic dimension of this function: IRDAI designates LIC as a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer every year, describing it as an institution whose distress would cause significant dislocation in the financial system. That designation, rightly made on insurance-sector grounds, points toward a wider truth — the dislocation would extend into the sovereign borrowing programme itself.
Insurers in Japan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea are among the largest holders of their respective governments’ long-dated securities, not because regulation mandates it but because their liability profiles demand it. India’s life insurance sector is following the same path.
The fragility within the stability
India’s life insurance penetration stood at 2.7 per cent of GDP in FY25, the third consecutive year of decline from a pandemic-era peak of 3.2 per cent, against a global life average of 3.0 per cent. Three regulatory interventions between 2023 and 2024 — restructured distribution economics, taxation on certain high-value policies, and mandatory product repricing, simultaneously, has compressed new businesses. While each was defensible in isolation, their cumulative effect was adverse. The sector is recovering. But the episode illustrates a risk worth noting: when multiple regulatory actions compress new business at once, the household savings that would otherwise have flowed into the sovereign debt market through insurance, reduce or find shorter-duration homes elsewhere. The sovereign borrowing programme may not notice this in the short term. Over a decade, it would.
The unacknowledged pillar
Banking commands policy attention in proportion to its systemic importance. Insurance, which quietly holds close to a quarter of outstanding central government dated securities, does not.
The case for deeper insurance penetration is most often made in the language of household financial protection — the uninsured family, the inadequate sum assured, a mis-sold product or an unsettled claim. These are legitimate concerns. But there is a parallel case, made in the language of sovereign fiscal stability, that has not been fully articulated in public policy discourse. If the reliability of India’s domestic sovereign funding base is a macroeconomic priority given the scale of annual borrowing requirements, then the depth and health of the life insurance sector remain directly relevant to that priority.
(T.C. Suseel Kumar is a former Managing Director of LIC India. R Sudhakar is a former Chief Investment Officer and Executive Director of LIC India. The views expressed are personal.)

briefs.headline: ‘Trusting entrepreneurs key to India’s success’
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: 
Anil Agarwal
, the billionaire-entrepreneur with his origin in Patna in Bihar, is putting in place a plan that would see every Vedanta group company being managed by professionals, and not by any of his family members. The majority ownership of these companies, however, would remain with the group’s London-listed company in which the family has majority ownership. Agarwal has set a $100-billion market capitalisation target for the group companies together for the short term, up from about $55 billion now. And, he also wants at least 35% of the group’s workforce to be women, up from 22% now.
Agarwal, who completed 50 years of his entrepreneurial journey this year, spoke to TOI. Excerpts:
Turning into an entrepreneur over 50 years ago
I came to Bombay (now Mumbai) from Patna in end-1975. In Patna, my father had a factory for iron grill gates and aluminium conductors. I worked there with him for five years and learnt the trade. In those days children in business families used to work from a very early age, alongside their studies. I started at 14.
First public listing for a group company
We listed Sterlite Cable and continued to grow the company. We started with cable, then set up a copper rod plant in Lonavala, and later set up a copper smelter in Tuticorin in the south. We used imported technology and machinery for these plants. 
That was the turning point.
Going global...
In 1989, we made our first attempt to settle abroad. We stayed in New York for four years but did not find much success. Then in 1991, the Narasimha Rao govt came to power in India. During his time, the licence raj was abolished. And in 1992-93, we came back to India, set up a jelly-filled cable factory, and there was a lot of growth. Then, in 1995, we acquired another factory in London, named Dura-Tube, for $3 million, ran it for a few years and then sold it for $7 million. After that, when we went to London, it took us three or four years.
The metals empire and more...
Currently, across the listed and unlisted entities, we have 10 major companies. We have very large operations in aluminium, copper, zinc, lead, silver and some other metals. We also have a very large renewable business. Our transmission business is also very strong.
Management’s visions and style...
Our vision is that, given our present position, our market cap will reach $100 billion in about a year or two. And in the long term each of these companies have the potential to become $50–100 billion companies. As for the management style, professionals will run the companies on an incentive basis. Our foreign company, owned by the family, will hold 54% in each of the ten companies. There should be a legacy of building very good companies with strong rules and regulations. Another goal of mine is, across all our businesses women should constitute 35% of the workforce. At present, our group’s revenue is around $30 billion. In two years, it should be $50 billion. And over the next three years, we are investing $25 billion to expand what we are doing. It is a very large investment, and once this is completed, our overall capacity will more than double.
On changing business environment in India
India is a country where people are born entrepreneurs. The more you trust and support them, the more the country will progress and the more employment will be created. That is the key.

briefs.headline: Global AI companies turn to India for data centre capacity
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Global AI companies are using Indian data centres to serve customers overseas, not just local users, as delays in securing power and capacity elsewhere push them to spread their computing infrastructure across countries, operators told TOI.
“We are already hosting some customers and have contracted large capacities with some of them,” said Sunil Gupta, co-founder, CEO and MD of Yotta Data Services, which operates data centres and rents out AI computing capacity.
“We are seeing international AI customers use infrastructure hosted and operated from India to serve workloads beyond the country,” he said.
At CtrlS Datacenters, which houses customers’ servers, discussions can begin with a requirement for 20 megawatts of capacity and quickly turn to expanding it to 100MW or more, said founder and CEO Sridhar Pinnapureddy. “AI is compressing the time available to respond while increasing the scale we need to build for. Higher power densities and advanced cooling must be planned alongside land, transmission, and future expansion,” he said.
