briefs.headline: West Asia crisis: Government ready with energy, fertiliser stocks
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: As war clouds gather over West Asia once again, govt seems better prepared with energy and fertiliser stocks, but higher oil prices will hurt the currency and deficit levels, apart from foreign portfolio investment, which is already under strain.
Besides, the already-elevated freight rates — nearly 10 times the pre-war level on certain routes — will spike further as insurance premiums rise in an environment when finding vessels and crew to go into the Strait of Hormuz is often difficult. This will have an impact on exports as well as the entire supply chain when container shortages are seen in the eastern hemisphere, along with port congestion in certain parts of the world.
On Oct 22, the Drewry World Container Index was at $4,585 for a 40-feet container, compared with $1,746 on Oct 25, 2025.
“It is already pushing freight rates beyond a point. Right now, buyers are managing because they were short of inventory. Now, that they are stocked up, it is unclear if they can absorb higher freight. Fresh disruption in West Asia will have an adverse impact for rest of the world too,” said Ajai Sahay, director general at Fieo. 
He said container rates to West Asian ports have shot up from $800 to $8,000 to $10,000 now.
“The East-West container freight market remains uncertain. Security risks and attacks on ships continue to affect vessel movements through the Gulf, with only two containerships sailing into the Gulf in Week 42, down from five the previous week. Meanwhile, sailings through the Suez Canal increased slightly, from 54 in Week 41 to 55 in Week 42,” Drewry said.
There are also concerns over crew and vessels entering the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as the epicentre of the conflict. In any case, most businesses reckon that any uncertainty, especially a war that has implications on global energy supplies, is best avoided.
Oil is the biggest concern with crude price for Indian refiners averaging $120 a barrel in Oct, the highest monthly average in 12 years. And, with petrol averaging $140 a barrel and diesel at over $154, the pressure on state-run retailers in mounting as they incur losses, given that pump prices are linked to the import price of the product.
Although govt had shielded them through duty cuts and permission to raise prices subsequently, the Centre has limited headroom for fiscal concessions. Already, fuel and fertiliser subsidies are well past last year’s level and it will have to provide extra, if the need arises.
For the moment, top officials said, fertiliser companies took advantage of a falling price window to stock up for the next season and the fertiliser ministry had some surplus cash with it due to the savings.
There is some cushion for the Centre due to higher-than-budgeted disinvestment receipts and dividends from state-run financial institutions and RBI, with tax collections holding up so far, which is expected to keep the fiscal deficit within the target of 4.3% of GDP. But, a spike in the import bill due to higher commodity prices will have impact on the trade deficit and the current account deficit. And, a weaker rupee will make it less attractive for foreign funds to invest in Indian stocks.

briefs.headline: Keeping all data centres sovereign, says RBI governor
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Information technology has become a core function of RBI, with secure, sovereign data centres and cybersecurity capabilities increasingly critical to the resilience of the financial system as AI transforms technology, governor Sanjay Malhotra said.
In an interview with Doordarshan following the inauguration of RBI’s new data centre and Cybersecurity Training Institute in Bhubaneswar by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Malhotra said the central bank needed to strengthen its technological infrastructure while keeping pace with emerging technologies.
“IT no longer is a support function. It is a very core function because it is from where all our applications for the general public, for our own use, and for consumers run,” he said.
The data centre will host applications supporting critical payment systems (NEFT & RTGS), govt banking operations and services for consumers of regulated financial entities. While the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) operates the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), settlement ultimately takes place through the data centres and applications built by RBI, Malhotra said.
The sovereign data centre, with four independent facilities and Tier IV accreditation, will improve efficiency, uptime and resilience. 
RBI has also applied for a platinum green-building rating, using local materials to blend with the surroundings. Two-thirds of the Bhubaneswar site houses a cybersecurity training institute, reflecting AI-driven security risks.
Inaugurating the facility, PM Modi stressed secure digital infrastructure and technological self-reliance. Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said it would house critical systems, including RTGS/NEFT, while building expertise in cybersecurity and emerging technologies. RBI aims to strengthen indigenous technology in support of India’s 2047 development goal.

briefs.headline: Banks pass on rate hikes, but go slow when rates fall; RBI study finds
briefs.deck: A recent study by the RBI indicates that banks are more responsive to interest rate hikes than to cuts. Specifically, banks relayed 76.4% of repo rate increases, while only 64% of reductions were passed on. Amid periods of tightening, lending rates surged significantly, in contrast to the minimal decreases observed during easing. This research highlights the intricate dynamics of interest rate…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: A study by 
RBI
 has found that interest rates adjust upward more completely during a tightening phase than they do downward during an easing phase.
According to the study, published in RBI Bulletin, banks passed on 76.4% of the 
repo rate
 increase through contract repricing, with lending rates rising by 191 basis points following a 250-basis-point hike between March 2022 and Jan 2025.
During the easing phase between Feb 2025 and March 2026, they passed on only 64% of the rate reduction, with lending rates falling by 80 basis points following a 125-basis-point cut. The study, titled ‘Transmission to Lending Rates of SCBs: Price versus Composition Effects in WALR’, notes that changes in the weighted average lending rate (WALR) reflect both changes in lending rates and shifts in loan-book composition.
While monetary policy pass-through to contracted loan rates was notably lower during the easing cycle (64%) than in the tightening cycle (76.4%), this gap narrowed significantly when evaluating the headline WALR—which captures shifts in credit composition—narrowing the pass-through disparity to 74.4% in the easing phase compared to 72.4% during tightening. During tightening, the 250-basis-point hike resulted in a 181-basis-point increase in WALR, and during easing, the 125 bps cut resulted in a 93 bps decline in the average rate.
During easing cycles, banks protect net interest margins (NIMs) by raising spreads or shifting towards higher-yielding loans, weakening rate-cut transmission. In March 2026, fresh lending rates rose 12 basis points despite the easing stance, according to RBI researchers Yuvraj Kashyap, Kamal Gupta and Arvind Jha.
MSME loans had the biggest impact on fresh-loan WALR, with rates falling 122 basis points during the Feb 2025-March 2026 easing cycle, against a 125-basis-point repo cut. For MSMEs, benchmark-linked repricing accounted for 118 basis points, reducing system-wide WALR by 24 basis points, over 2.6 times any other sector’s contribution.
Education loan rates fell the most, by 162 basis points, but contributed virtually nothing to the overall WALR decline because of their small share of credit. Rupee export credit rates fell 161 basis points but contributed just five basis points. Large-industry rates fell 67 basis points, contributing nine basis points to the decline; a nine-basis-point positive weight effect, reflecting shifts towards higher-spread loans or lenders, partly offset the pressure.

briefs.headline: IndiGo, Air India to shift flights to Navi Mumbai as Mumbai airport prepares Terminal 1 redevelopment
briefs.deck: In a separate statement, the Air India group said it “will progressively transition Air India Express services to Jeddah, Riyadh, Dammam, Doha, Muscat, and Sharjah, to NMIA, with the process expected to be completed by the IATA Northern Summer 2027 season”
briefs.bodyText:
IndiGo and Air India Group will progressively shift flights from Mumbai’s existing airport to the newly built Navi Mumbai International Airport from December, clearing capacity for the redevelopment of Terminal 1 and paving the way for a dual-airport system in the country’s financial capital.
The coordinated transition, planned in phases through the 2027 summer aviation season, will move selected domestic and international services to Navi Mumbai while allowing airlines to retain their historical operating slots at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA), the airport operators and airlines said.
The shift follows nearly 18 months of consultations between airlines and Adani Airport Holdings Ltd, which operates both Mumbai airports. It reflects growing airline participation in the new airport’s operational ramp-up and is intended to ease capacity constraints at CSMIA while accommodating rising air traffic.
“IndiGo will progressively transfer 12 daily international departures from Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA) to NMIA, representing all the present operations from CSMIA to Bahrain, Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah, Madinah, Kuwait, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah, Muscat, Dhaka and Jakarta.
“An additional daily service to Kathmandu will also be introduced, taking IndiGo’s international network at NMIA to 12 destinations between February and July 2027,” a joint statement by IndiGo and the airport said.
In a separate statement, the Air India group said it “will progressively transition Air India Express services to Jeddah, Riyadh, Dammam, Doha, Muscat, and Sharjah, to NMIA, with the process expected to be completed by the IATA Northern Summer 2027 season.”
This transition, it said, is a result of continued collaborative engagement with the airport operator and is aligned with the wider airport transition programme for both Indian and international airlines and will support the long-awaited redevelopment of CSMIA Terminal 1. “The phased move also supports the development of Mumbai’s dual-airport system while enabling Air India Group to continue serving the market efficiently and preserve the historicity of its existing operating slots at CSMIA.”
Operating from both CSMIA and NMIA will strengthen connectivity across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, provide travellers with greater choice and convenience, and support the continued growth of aviation infrastructure in the region, the statement said.
“Adani Airport Holdings Limited welcomed Air India Group’s plans to commence operations from NMIA. Navi Mumbai International Airport is being developed with advanced technology, multimodal connectivity and scalable infrastructure to support the region’s future aviation growth and deliver a seamless travel experience,” it added.
IndiGo will also shift supporting domestic connectivity to facilitate international transfers at the new airport. The airline and Adani Airports are in the final stages of operational planning, with final transition dates subject to project coordination and operating approvals.
The capacity released at CSMIA will help IndiGo introduce new international services across Asia, Africa and Europe in 2027, using its expanding A320/A321 and A321XLR fleet. Further adjustments to its operations at Terminal 1 to facilitate redevelopment are expected to be accommodated at Terminal 2.
IndiGo will also transition the required domestic connectivity from CSMIA to NMIA to support these international services from CSMIA to NMIA, ensuring seamless onward connections for customers.
“In close collaboration with IndiGo, AAHL has been working to enable the necessary infrastructure at NMIA for delivering a smooth and efficient transfer experience between IndiGo’s International and Domestic services at NMIA,” their joint statement said. “This will mark the next step of IndiGo’s expansion strategy to build NMIA as a long-term international hub.”
At CSMIA, this capacity transition will also facilitate two additional joint objectives. First, it will create room for IndiGo’s continued international expansion in 2027, enabling the launch of new services across Asia, Africa and Europe using its expanding fleet of A320/321 and A321XLR during 2027, without placing further pressure on a capacity-constrained airport.
Second, the associated transition of domestic operations will also support IndiGo’s share of the capacity reductions required to enable the redevelopment of CSMIA T1 by 2030. “IndiGo and AAHL will continue to work together to ensure that any further adjustments required to IndiGo’s services at CSMIA T1, to enable the redevelopment, will be accommodated in CSMIA T2,” it said.
The statement went on to state that the phased transition is intended to support a transparent, equitable and proportionate rebalancing of capacity across Mumbai’s dual airport system, taking into account each airline’s presence at CSMIA. “This balanced approach will help facilitate an orderly transition for all carriers, minimize operational disruption and provide greater planning certainty for airlines and passengers as NMIA scales up and CSMIA progresses with its redevelopment.”
IndiGo will announce final dates for the transition of services to NMIA and introduction of new services to CSMIA after completion of final project coordination and relevant operating approvals are secured, the statement added.
The planned transfer of around 3 million passengers — accounting for approximately 60% of the traffic targeted for relocation in the first phase — will create the necessary headroom for the phased redevelopment of CSMIA’s Terminal 1. The initial phase aims to shift approximately 5 million passengers to Navi Mumbai, enabling critical safety enhancements, modernisation, upgraded passenger facilities and expanded handling capacity at CSMIA.
CSMIA handles around 55 million passengers annually, and the operator says about 91 per cent of its traffic will continue to operate from the existing airport during the redevelopment programme. The temporary relocation is intended to create the headroom needed to modernise Terminal 1 without disrupting the bulk of Mumbai’s air traffic.
The redevelopment is expected to raise Terminal 1’s annual passenger-handling capacity by about 33 per cent, from 15 million to 20 million. Planned upgrades include safety enhancements, modernised passenger facilities and improved digital and processing systems.
The airport operator has said airlines’ historical CSMIA slots will be restored after the redevelopment is completed. The transition is also intended to distribute capacity more proportionately between the two airports, taking account of each airline’s existing presence at CSMIA, and to provide carriers with greater certainty in planning future operations.
Navi Mumbai International Airport is designed to handle 20 million passengers annually in its initial phase, with future expansion planned to take capacity to 90 million. Its infrastructure includes automated baggage handling, digital passenger-processing systems and road links serving business districts, logistics hubs and other centres across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Further multimodal transport connections are planned.
The development of two airports is intended to expand Mumbai’s overall aviation capacity, improve domestic-international connections and create room for more international routes and carriers. A larger network could also help the city attract more transfer traffic, strengthening its role as an international gateway.
For airlines, the transition offers an opportunity to expand services without placing additional pressure on an already capacity-constrained CSMIA. For passengers, it promises a broader choice of flights over time, but the phased relocation will make it important to check departure airports carefully when booking and before travelling.
The planned moves by IndiGo and Air India Group mark a significant step in that transition, creating the operational space needed to modernise CSMIA while building Navi Mumbai into a larger domestic and international aviation hub.

briefs.headline: ‘Excess’: Insured, but still responsible
briefs.deck: The NCB rewards claim-free years, either through a discount on renewal premium or an increase in the sum insured, depending on the type of policy.
briefs.bodyText:
In the previous instalment of Cover Note (October 5, 2026, Policy ‘excess’ does not mean more for you), we saw that an excess or deductible means the first portion of an admissible claim that you must bear yourself.
But why excess? In a motor policy covering a ₹20 lakh car, what difference does a few thousand rupees make? Why do some health policies require a co-payment?
One reason, as we saw, is to discourage small claims and reduce the time and administrative costs of processing them.
Suppose your excess is ₹1,000 and your loss is ₹2,500. You may decide that making a ₹1,500 claim isn’t worth the trouble, or you may go ahead. The excess thus influences not only how much the insurer pays, but also whether a claim is made at all.
No-claim bonus
There is another reason to think twice before making small claims, especially under motor and health policies. It has nothing to do with excess. It is the no-claim bonus, or NCB.
The NCB rewards claim-free years, either through a discount on renewal premium or an increase in the sum insured, depending on the type of policy. And this matters to you because making a claim may mean losing some or all of the accumulated bonus.
Consider a car policy with an annual own-damage (OD) premium of ₹10,000 before NCB and an accumulated bonus of 50%. You would normally pay ₹5,000 for the OD renewal, assuming the base premium remains unchanged. But if you make an admissible own-damage claim, even for ₹2,000, you could lose the entire NCB and have to pay ₹10,000 instead.
That is ₹5,000 in lost discount for a claim of ₹2,000!
When to make a claim
So, you should make a claim only if what you stand to receive exceeds the no-claim bonus.
Of course, health insurance NCB provisions work differently, and some motor policies offer NCB protection. So, check your policy to see what happens to your bonus when you claim. Compare the possible loss of NCB with the amount you stand to receive and make an informed decision.
But excess serves a purpose beyond discouraging small claims.
Insurance is founded, among other things, on the expectation that the insured will behave as a prudent uninsured — taking reasonable care to prevent losses and minimise their consequences.
Just as the insurer is your partner in misfortune, you should endeavour to be its partner in good fortune by making every reasonable effort to avoid losses. An excess reinforces this responsibility. By ensuring that you bear a portion of the loss, it gives you a financial interest in preventing it. You are encouraged to be as careful with the insurer’s money as you would be with your own.
It is somewhat like the margin you contribute when taking a housing loan. The lender finances most of the purchase, but your own money is also at stake.
Specified risks
The larger idea is that insurance is not intended to take every financial consequence of every loss off your hands. It provides protection against specified risks, while leaving you responsible for the portion you have agreed to retain.
An excess, therefore, is not necessarily a shortcoming in insurance protection. It is part of how that protection is designed.
(The writer is a business journalist specialising in insurance and corporate history)

stories.headline: 'What did I do wrong?': Ex-India star reveals how being dropped from team pushed him into depression
stories.deck: Amit Mishra faced significant challenges after being excluded from the Indian cricket team for an extended period. He battled depression for 18 months, questioning his performance while continuing to play. A conversation with a selector helped him realize he needed to improve his domestic performance to succeed. After reflecting on his situation, he managed to return to the Indian team in 2008.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Being dropped from the Indian team was one of the toughest phases of 
Amit Mishra
's cricket career. The former India leg-spinner has revealed that he battled depression for 18 months because he could not understand why he was not getting chances to play for the country.
Mishra made his international debut in 2003. However, he soon found himself out of the Indian team. He was also not picked for some domestic tournaments. Despite continuing to play cricket, he kept wondering why he was being left out.
Speaking to former India batter Aakash Chopra, Mishra opened up about how the setback affected him.
“I went into depression for a year and a half. I kept thinking about what my mistake was. I was playing everywhere, but the only question in my mind was that, ‘what did I do wrong?’" Mishra said.
A selector's advice helped Amit Mishra
Mishra was also left out of the Duleep Trophy and the India A zonal setup. He struggled to understand why he was not getting opportunities until a selector spoke to him about his performances.
“Then a selector told me that I was not performing. I sat down and thought, and I understood that I was thinking of playing for India itself but not performing in domestic cricket," he recalled.
The selector's words made Mishra think about his approach. He realised that he was thinking too much about returning to the Indian team and not focusing enough on performing in domestic cricket.
Mishra returned to domestic circuit, worked on his game, and his performances eventually helped him return to the Indian team in 2008, almost five years after his debut.
He went on to play 22 Tests, 36 ODIs and 10 T20Is for India. He claimed taking 156 wickets across the three formats.

stories.headline: IND A vs NZ A: Padikkal hits ton as India A take lead after first-innings collapse
stories.bodyText:
What a knock from Devdutt Padikkal! The left-hander continued his brilliant batting display to help India A take their lead past 100 runs.
India A reached 306 for 4 in 78.3 overs in the second session, stretching their lead to 102 runs after being bowled out for just 113 in the first innings.
Padikkal batting on 171 off 219 balls, with 21 fours and two sixes. He has led India's recovery with a superb innings after the team lost early wickets.
Yash Rathod is unbeaten on 26 off 33 balls, including three fours.
The pair will look to extend their partnership and help India A build a bigger lead as the day progresses.
Devdutt Padikkal has stepped up the scoring as India A look to build a strong lead against New Zealand A.
Padikkal went after Jayden Lennox in the 73rd over, hitting a six over long-on and following it up with a four towards backward square leg. The left-hander has raised his scoring rate as India A look to put more runs on the board.
Padikkal was unbeaten on 144 off 196 balls, with 18 fours and two sixes. Yash Rathod was batting on 14 off 20 balls, with India A reaching 267 for 4 in 72.3 overs.
India A now lead by 63 runs, with Padikkal looking well set to make the most of his innings.
WICKET!
Dhruv Jurel fell for two after playing a poor shot against Zak Gibson. Gibson bowled a short delivery that climbed on Jurel, but the India A batter went for the hook shot and got a top edge. Substitute fielder Jarrod McKay, positioned at backward square leg, kept his eyes on the swirling ball and dived to his left to complete the catch.
Jurel, who is usually effective with his pull shots, was late on this occasion and had to walk back to the pavilion.
Dhruv Jurel c (sub) Jarrod McKay b Zak Gibson 2 (12).
Devdutt Padikkal scored a century to put India A in front against New Zealand A.
New Zealand A were bowled out for 317 in their first innings, while India A managed only 113 in response. However, India A fought back strongly in their second innings, reaching 228 for 4 in 66 overs in the second session on Day 3.
India A now lead by 24 runs.
Padikkal remained unbeaten on 118 off 172 balls, hitting 15 fours and one six. Yash Rathod was unbeaten on one off five balls at the other end.
India A lost their fourth wicket when Dhruv Jurel was caught by substitute fielder Jarrod McKay off Zak Gibson for two off 12 balls. The dismissal came at 227 in 65.1 overs.
Gibson had figures of 1 for 39 in 12 overs, including three maiden overs, while Jayden Lennox conceded 38 runs in seven overs without taking a wicket.
Padikkal and Rathod had added one run for the fifth wicket at the time of the latest update.

stories.headline: Harmanpreet, Deepti on fire as India seals emphatic series win against Zimbabwe
stories.bodyText:
Picture this. Harmanpreet Kaur and Deepti Sharma scored centuries to power India to a big win. Now ask yourself: which of the two blazed her way to triple figures? If your gut said Harmanpreet, it failed you.
On a sweltering Sunday at the BCA Stadium in Kotambi, the second ODI against Zimbabwe turned the script on its head. A restrained Harmanpreet played the artisan while Deepti played destroyer, with their record-breaking 153-run fifth-wicket stand laying the foundation of India’s 121-run win and unassailable 2-0 lead.
India was stuttering at 19 for two in the third over — Smriti Mandhana and Shafali Verma both undone by Nomvelo Sibanda’s short-ball ploy — when Harmanpreet joined Pratika Rawal.
Pratika, fresh from a hundred in the first ODI, and Harmanpreet added 124 off 118 balls. The former looked set for another ton when Nyasha Gwanzura deceived her with a change of pace. Tejal Hasabnis followed soon after.
But Harmanpreet remained unfazed, aided by a fearless Deepti who arrived as if stepping in for a net session.
As many as 32 of the pair’s first 47 runs came through Deepti’s audacious shots on the leg-side while Harmanpreet whipped out a catalogue of puritanical drives and cuts on the off-side.
When the century came, celebrations oddly didn’t. Neither did tears, like the 91 she scored in the third T20I had drawn out of her. Deepti, too, eventually braved a slowdown to reach her second ODI century in the final over — nine years after her first — helping India set an intimidating 329-run target.
Modester Mupachikwa’s sprightly start, despite losing Loryn Phiri early, gave Zimbabwe hope.
With support from Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano, the Lady Chevrons got to 100 in just 19 overs, helped by India’s worrying inability to take wickets, especially the seamers. Sayali Satghare finally succeeded in breaching Mugeri-Tiripano’s defence.
Left-arm spinner Vaishnavi Sharma’s guile and persistence then took centrestage. She removed Mupachikwa for her maiden ODI wicket before dismissing Beloved Biza, Michelle Mavunga and skipper Josephine Nkomo in a cluster.
Deepti ran through the tail before Jintimani Kalita opened her account in the format.
While Zimbabwe ticked one box by crossing 200, its bid to last the full 50 overs was yet to be achieved.
The scores: India 328/6 in 50 overs (Pratika Rawal 61, Harmanpreet Kaur 126, Deepti Sharma 106 n.o.) bt Zimbabwe 207 in 48.5 overs (Modester Mupachikwa 49, Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano 46, Beloved Biza 34, Deepti 3/32, Vaishnavi Sharma 4/39).
Toss: India; PoM: Harmanpreet.

stories.headline: Tilak —the yo-yo man of India’sT20 set-up
stories.deck: Like Kohli during a chase, he somehow swaps his brain for a computer; he works out angles and areas to target and bowlers to attack, mentally recalibrating with every passing over and somehow insulating himself from the rising levels of panic that manifest themselves in addled decision-making when push comes to shove
stories.bodyText:
Versatility is a wonderful virtue to possess in any sphere of life. To be very good at more than one discipline is a grand trait not bestowed upon many. True, one must work unbelievably hard to maximise that gift, but as they say in a sporting parlance, primarily, you make your own luck.
Versatility can also be counter-productive, especially in a setting like a team sport. And in the context of Indian cricket, specifically.
Take Rahul Dravid as a case in point. Because he was so adept at so many different and often unrelated aspects, he was moved out of his comfort zone so many times that towards the end, even he may not have been sure what his comfort zone was. Need someone to fill the breach in Test cricket as an opener? Hey, there’s Rahul, you know. Need someone to drop down the order to accommodate a more attacking option at No. 3, as famously happened at the Eden game against Australia in 2001? Don’t look beyond Rahul. Looking for a dependable ‘finisher’ in 50-over internationals, long before that term became fashionable? Surely, Rahul? Require a gun batter to also don the wicketkeeping gloves because it can extend the batting order, provide a specialist option at No. 7 and not affect the balance one bit? Hello, wasn’t Rahul a wicketkeeper at school?
The same path
It’s amazing how his namesake from the same city has walked pretty much the same path. K.L. Rahul is the modern-day equivalent of Rahul Dravid, having donned each of the roles his illustrious predecessor did during a wonderful career that ran between 1995 and 2012. In those 17 years, just about the only thing Dravid didn’t do was keep wickets to his own bowling – he even took two wickets in an over in an ODI against South Africa in Kochi in March 2000, getting rid of left-handers Gary Kirsten and Lance Klusener with his off-spin. Perhaps the only reason ‘KL’ doesn’t have an international wicket is that successive captains from Mahendra Singh Dhoni to Shubman Gill, himself included, haven’t yet summoned him to the bowling crease.
Tilak Varma hasn’t done all of the above things – he hasn’t even made his Test debut or opened the batting in white-ball internationals, though he does boast five T20I wickets – but he is fast emerging as the ultimate yo-yo man of the current T20I set-up. India’s vice-captain in the 20-over format provides the classic case of being asked to play the situation.
He doesn’t have a fixed batting position even though he has made no secret of the fact that his preferred slot is No. 3, from where he has uncorked both his international centuries. Forget about fixed, there is no guarantee that he will occupy the same berth for two games in a row – indeed, he has batted at a different slot in each of his last three innings – and yet, that hasn’t come in the way of an average of 44.13 and a strike-rate of 147.47 after 68 T20I innings.
Virat Kohli is acknowledged as the ultimate chaser in white-ball history and it is hard to argue with that tag, given how many times he has made the impossible look commonplace. But how is this for a stat? Tilak has remained unbeaten in 26 chases in all T20s, 12 of them in country vs country battles, and finished on the winning side every single time. What do you make of that, Virat?
The wirily elegant left-hander’s latest masterpiece came at the Hagley Oval in Christchurch on Saturday, in a match few believed was headed India’s way. New Zealand’s 180 for five was already a lot more than it read numerically, and assumed even more gargantuan proportions after India played themselves into a hole at 70 for five, skipper Mitchell Santner accounting for three of those wickets with his parsimonious, penetrative left-arm spin.
Tilak had walked in at 69 for four and taken a single off his first delivery from Santner, only for Axar Patel to be dismissed next ball, caught at long-on. India needed 111 off 55 deliveries with Tilak one ball young, and Naman Dhir and Nitish Kumar to follow. The odds of them pulling off a second consecutive stiff run-chase were pretty long.
But over the last year or so particularly, the 23-year-old Tilak has showcased a skillset that is clearly out of the ordinary. Like Kohli during a chase, he somehow swaps his brain for a computer, working out angles and areas to target and bowlers to attack, mentally recalibrating with every passing over and somehow insulating himself from the rising levels of panic that manifest themselves in addled decision-making when push comes to shove.
Instant hero
The Hyderabadi had become an instant hero to millions in September last year when he wrenched the T20 Asia Cup final rudely out of Pakistan’s hands. In the third successive Sunday showdown between the sides in the desert sands of Dubai, Pakistan seemed on course to avenge defeats over the two previous weekends and win the match that mattered the most by having India on the mat at 20 for three in response to their 146 all out, courtesy a dramatic meltdown that saw them lose their last nine wickets for 33 runs after looking good for 180, at the very least, at various stages.
Batting at No. 4, Tilak strung together a 57-run stand for the fourth wicket with a struggling, out-of-sorts Sanju Samson (24 off 21) before finding excellent support from the vastly underrated Shivam Dube. The tall left-hander contributed 33 in an alliance of 60 but when he departed off the last ball of the penultimate over, a nervy India still needed 10 with the speedy but profligate Haris Rauf thrown the ball by Salman Agha.
Tilak settled all the nerves with a thumping six off the second ball, smearing the short offering over the deep backward square-leg fence for a resounding six. Rinku Singh applied the finishing touches but there was no disputing who the real hero was. Tilak finished undefeated on 69 off 53 with only three fours and four sixes, but the timing of those boundaries complemented his hard running superbly as India pulled the fat out of the fire with something to spare.
The stakes were just as high in Nisshin earlier this month when India faced their arch-rivals, again, in the final of the Asian Games. This time, India batted first and seemed to have sold themselves a few short, despite opener Abhishek Sharma’s blazing 28-ball 61, when Tilak exploded in a frenzy of fours and sixes. Batting at No. 6, he reached his 50 off a mere 21 deliveries, helping India amass a frenetic 78 runs off the last 35 deliveries of the innings, a decisive contribution given that their final margin of victory was 19 runs.
In Christchurch on Saturday, there was just a straightforward victory – how extraordinarily naively simplistic to put it thus – on the line. No Asia Cup trophy (which India are still to receive, lest it should be forgotten), no Asian Games gold medal. Just a regular, regulation win and the chance to go 2-0 up with three to play, But this was neither a straightforward, nor a regular and regulation task, not with the top five back in the hut and Tilak having to make do with only Nos. 7 and 8 for meaningful company.
He wasn’t coming off a great immediate sequence of scores himself – 7 off 6 balls (at No. 5) in the rain-ruined game against West Indies in Bengaluru last Saturday, then 6 off 11 (at No. 3) in Thursday’s first T20I in Christchurch. His return to the middle-order was promoted by the adductor muscle injury to Ishan Kishan that brought Vaibhav Sooryavanshi into the XI at No. 3, but Tilak didn’t allow being tugged around repeatedly to faze him.
“I have said before that I want to finish games for the country,” Tilak had said in Bengaluru after the abandoned game. “I love doing that job. For me as an individual, it will be easier batting at No. 3 and finishing games. But Ishan is batting brilliantly at No. 3 and for me now, there is no option but to bat at 5 and 6 and do the job for the team.
Mentally prepared
“I am mentally prepared for that role. I have won a few games from there. As a finisher, most of the times in T20s, you will get a maximum of 5-6 overs to bat, so you have to play your strokes from ball one. I have batted up the order from my childhood, therefore I am confident that whether I bat at 3 and 5, I have got both the techniques where I can adapt (to the demands of each role).”
Perfect chasing template
As if to show that that was no empty boast, Tilak produced the perfect chasing template at the Hagley Oval. He also played it smart. Knowing that spin was doing the trick for New Zealand and that therefore to attempt anything outrageous against Santner and offie Michael Bracewell was nothing if not foolhardy, he bided his time, waiting for pace to be brought back into the attack. He didn’t, however, let the spinners apply the choke. First with the increasingly impressive Dhir and then with Nitish, Tilak ran wonderfully well between the wickets, using the dimensions of the ground to such great advantage that you could have been forgiven for mistakenly believing that he had played all his cricket at the Hagley.
Even when the task became more and more difficult – 46 needed off the last three overs – Tilak kept his wits about him. By now, Dhir had perished after a terrific cameo, 31 off 17, but Nitish was chugging along nicely. Tilak switched gears without seeming to, two fours in the 18th over (from Jacob Duffy) the precursor to three fours and a six from the next, sent down by Nathan Smith. That brought the equation down to a manageable 11 off the last over and Tilak calmly battered Duffy’s second ball wide of mid-off for four to practically finish off the chase.
By the time Nitish formally heralded victory, Tilak had conjured a 25-ball half-century and reiterated his chasing credentials. No. 3 might be his favourite position, but how can he expect to get a sustained run there when he is so good at No. 5 and 6 and 7 when he refuses to take a backward step. Tilak is working zealously on the approach – batting-wise and mentally – needed in the middle order, and is well on his way to mastering it. To say that he won’t be occupying the No. 3 slot on even a semi-permanent basis in a hurry is no exaggeration, but no one, not even he, is complaining.

briefs.headline: Denso Iris reigns supreme
briefs.bodyText:
The best part about Denso Iris (Japan) is that it does not rely solely on its foreign imports, unlike most teams in the FIBA Women’s Basketball League Asia at the Sree Kanteerava Indoor Stadium here. Instead, it thrives on collective effort, with every player contributing and the foreigners complementing the team’s overall game.
On Sunday, in the final against favourite Sichuan Yuanda Meile (China), Iris underlined the strength of that approach.
Iris’s commanding 81-63 victory over the Chinese side was a powerful vindication of its philosophy.
Sichuan, heavily dependent on American Chennedy Carter and Australian Sara Blicavs, struggled to find its attacking rhythm. Carter was disqualified early in the second quarter after picking up two technical fouls, while Blicavs was not at her best. With Iris’s defence denying it the space to operate freely, Sichuan found it increasingly difficult to raise the tempo.
Iris’ disciplined approach and sustained intensity were reflected in the way it built its advantage quarter after quarter, moving from 24-20 after the first quarter to 43-36 at half-time before sealing an 81-63 victory.
Maki Takada, a three-time Olympian at 37 years was a striking example of experience triumphing over age. Neither exceptionally quick nor overly aggressive, the veteran centre relied on composure, sound positioning to finish as the game’s top scorer with 23 points, including seven two-pointers and a three-pointer.
G. Parameshwar, Deputy Chief Minister of Karnataka, gave away the prizes.

briefs.deck: Fresh from their innings victory against Odisha in their last match, Kerala will have a job in hand to stop an upbeat Bengal who will be looking for a hat-trick of wins after beating Delhi and Services to lie at the top of the table with 12 points in their group.
briefs.bodyText:
If momentum is important in sports, then both Kerala and Bengal will carry it in abundance when they face each other in an Elite Group C 
Ranji Trophy
 match at the KCA ground, Mangalapuram, in 
Thiruvananthapuram
 on Monday.
Fresh from their innings victory against Odisha in their last match, Kerala will have a job in hand to stop an upbeat Bengal who will be looking for a hat-trick of wins after beating Delhi and Services to lie at the top of the table with 12 points in their group.
However, Bengal will look for an improved show from their batters after they failed to put up enough runs on board against Services. It was their spinners who did the job for them then, but the KCA ground is unlikely to assist the spinners much. In that case Bengal might go in with three pacers, with 
Mohammed Shami
 once again taking up the new ball after the former India pacer sat out in the last game. He will expect good support from his brother Mohammed Kaif and Suraj Singh Jaiswal. Toss is likely to play an important role on a surface which offers early assistance to the pacers.
Bengal coach Laxmi Ratan Shukla will look for more runs from the blades of Sudip Chatterjee and opener Ankur Pal as Bengal need to put up a competitive total against a good batting unit that features Sachin Baby, Vishnu Vinod and Mohammed Azharuddin. 
Much will depend on how the ever-dependent Jalaj Saxena contributes both with the ball and bat.
Shahbaz Ahmed will once again play a key role for Bengal, after the all-rounder made an immediate impact on returning from an injury to play his first match in months against Services.
However, the weather might play spoiler, with forecasts of occasional rain, which ruined the teams’ practice sessions, over the next few days. But the possibility of a complete washout is remote, and both sides are preparing for a stop-start game.

briefs.headline: Women's India Open: Vani Kapoor makes herself heard but Phatlum has last word
briefs.deck: Indian Finishes Second As Thai Invitee Makes It Four Triumphs At Women's Indian Open
briefs.bodyText:
GURUGRAM
: The autumn leaves were falling on the vantage point, where many had gathered for a glimpse of the ninth hole at DLF G&CC. Overnight leader Vani Kapoor’s rousing birdie on the eighth kept her one ahead of the experienced Thai, Pornanong Phatlum, already a three-time winner at the venue, although on the old Arnold Palmer-designed layout.
People could sense a turning point as the LPGA golfer collected her fifth birdie of the day. The home pro stood over her small pressure putt, studying the lines over and over again, taking a step backwards, playing it in her mind, then attempting again. Finally she hit, it was a miss!
A leaf fell again on the shoulder. Was it nature’s way of saying that the hopes had withered too? The spectators remained still, in disbelief, then politely clapped in admiration as the calm Thai caught up with the home challenger.
Maybe that elusive Hero Women’s Indian Open trophy had slipped out of our hands again.
Onto the par-4 10th, and Vani’s second shot was short, and her wedge failed to find the right spot on the green. As Phatlum settled for her two-putt par, Vani's putter missed the target again for a bogey. The narrative had changed.
This is the club where Vani, a star student of the DLF Academy, had grown up. A casual walk here would often lead to one bumping into the little confident girl whose dreams were big. 
Older now at 32, her expectations were now tempered with a sprinkling of reality. But despite all the disappointments home and away, she carried on with a happy demeanour.
In golf, you could be second but you were still a winner but only one could walk away with the prize, and that person needed a little bit of luck, she had said before.
The stumbles on the back-nine ensured that Vani came second. Yes, she was still a winner. But champion Phatlum made her own luck. When the Indian came out, all irons blazing, with four birdies in five holes, the Thai managed three of her own, adding two more before the turn.
Pars can be powerful if you are ahead, and others are not making their moves. Phatlum was creating her own new chapter with two more birdies after the lull under the strong afternoon sun for a final-day bogey-free seven-under 65, and a magical fourth triumph by four strokes.
Vani quietly accepted her lot with her round of 70, as her bogey tumbles on the return journey set the tone for the unhappy conclusion. “I think this year I was much more confident, and more anchored. I had much more clarity in my head and a sense of purpose,” she shared her positive notes.
But she had felt the pressure. “Some shots you don’t have exactly have the yardage you want, and you have to think about where you can miss the ball. Those are stressful, so there were little mistakes there.”
But where the margins are minute, especially on the slopey greens of the Gary Player course, little could become large when you are fighting for the championship. “I don’t think I could have done anything more. I made a lot of birdies, especially considering the amount of pressure there was. I made a couple of mistakes too, but that’s part of the game.”
Golf can be cruel, it can also be rejuvenating.
For the petite Thai conqueror with an infectious smile, this is the end of a long drought.
Phatlum, who has returned to India after 14 years on an invite, had her first look at the changed environment and used all her experience on American shores to plot her way around the course where “every shot counts”.
With soft skills to match the Mudmee silk her hometown of Khon Kaen is famous for, Phatlum steadily improved with rounds of 72, 71, 69 as her understanding of the playground grew, to finish on a high of 65. With a solo second at the 2018 Women’s British Open in her resume, the Women’s Indian Open champion of 2008, 2009 and 2012 had seen better years on the LPGA. With the 2026 crown, her love affair with the tournament continued. “I think I could live in India,” the 36-year-old said, giggling.
Stomach bug Pranavi's biggest challenge
The Indians are getting closer to that hallowed trophy, which Aditi Ashok won in 2016.
A second place finish is as good as it gets for now. “It was Pornanong’s experience which came clutch today,” explained Pranavi Urs, who finished tied-fourth.
It was a week the Asian Games gold medallist was looking forward to. “With the way I’ve been playing, I thought I would have a chance.”
The biggest obstacle was not the course, but her stomach. Not having a proper meal since Pro-Am day, the breathless figure could be seen struggling as the day progressed. Despite the trouble, the Mysuru girl finished with a 72 and a total of three-under.
Tvesa Malik was the third Indian in the top-10, at 7th place.

briefs.headline: Sharath recalls five-year ‘fruitful journey’ as a national selector
briefs.bodyText:
For the last five years, S. Sharath has been a key member of the Indian cricket set-up, serving twice as chairman of the junior committee and three years as a senior selector.
During his stints, the India under-19 team won World Cups in 2022 and 2026, and he also helped select the senior squads that won the 2024 T20 World Cup and the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy.
“It has been a very fruitful journey to be able to contribute to Indian cricket. I missed out on playing for the country, but God has been kind enough to let me contribute in a different role.
“I am grateful for the support of N. Srinivasan sir, K.S. Viswanathan sir, Jay (bhai) Shah and my family,” said Sharath.
“It was a team effort, and I was blessed to work with some great former cricketers in both committees. I also have to mention Rahul Dravid and V.V.S. Laxman, and the CoE’s support.”
The former Tamil Nadu batter gave an insight into what makes a good selector. “First thing is you should disassociate yourself from the fact that you were a former player and come with an open mind. The game has evolved, and you should understand the demands of the team combination,” said the 53-year-old.
“Skills are always there, but it is the mental side of the game that is important. A selector must be empathetic. You have more bad days than good days as a player, and how you react on a bad day tells how good a player is.”
“If you are a batter, small things like whether he is switched on while at the non-striker’s end helping his partner or as a bowler whether he is running in hard through the day, these are things you observe.”
On the highlights of his tenure, “In 2021, when I took over as chairman, we were in the midst of a pandemic. Our young boys hadn’t played any cricket for two years. So, putting together a team in a short time and winning the World Cup was special. The highlight for me will be the 2023 ODI World Cup. Though we lost in the final, we were the dominant team in that tournament and played an exciting brand of cricket.”

briefs.headline: Acho Donations Fund Hospital: Former NFL star backs Nigeria clinic; $100,000 helped build it
briefs.deck: Since 1989, Sam Acho's family has been dedicated to providing free medical care to underserved populations in Nigeria. In June 2017, they established the Living Hope Medical Center, significantly funded by Acho's NFL award nominations, which raised $100,000. This funding facilitated a shift from temporary medical missions to a permanent facility, ensuring consistent healthcare access throughout…
briefs.bodyText:
Sam Acho’s family began providing free medical care in Nigeria in 1989. His parents, Dr. Sonny Acho and Christie Acho, wanted to help people who had limited access to healthcare. Their annual medical missions treated thousands of patients, but the teams could stay only for a short time. The family eventually began working toward a permanent medical center that could serve the community throughout the year.
Years later, Acho’s 
NFL
 career helped support that goal. His two nominations for the Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year Award in 2016 and 2017 brought a combined $100,000 in charitable donations. Acho directed the money to Living Hope Christian Ministries to help fund the hospital project. The Living Hope Medical Center opened in June 2017.
Sam Acho joined his parents’ medical mission as a teenager
Acho grew up in Dallas, Texas, but his family’s connection to Nigeria remained strong. His parents had spent years working to improve access to healthcare in the country, returning regularly to provide free treatment to people who struggled to find medical help.
Their work was organised through Living Hope Christian Ministries, founded by Acho’s father, Dr. Sonny Acho. The medical missions brought healthcare professionals to communities where local facilities often lacked basic resources. 
Doctors, nurses and other volunteers treated patients during visits that typically lasted around two weeks.
Acho joined his parents on a medical mission as a teenager. He was not there as a doctor. Instead, he helped with tasks such as crowd control and guiding patients through the treatment process. Seeing the conditions firsthand gave him a better understanding of the work his parents had taken on.
In a 2023 interview with the University of Texas at Austin, Acho recalled the makeshift facilities where the medical teams worked.
“They’d go to these ‘hospitals’ — I use quotes because they were really just abandoned buildings in the village — and they’d give out free medical care,” Acho said.
The teams treated thousands of people during their visits, but the need for healthcare continued after they left. Patients could receive help while the volunteers were in the country, yet many had nowhere reliable to turn for further treatment once the mission ended.
Acho’s father wanted to find a lasting solution. His vision was to build a permanent medical center that could provide care throughout the year. The family had spent years travelling to Nigeria and treating patients during short visits. A hospital would allow that work to continue between missions.
“This was the dream and vision of my dad,” Acho said. “We’d go for two weeks and treat as many people as we could — thousands of people. But we would leave, and people still needed help.”
The family began pursuing the hospital project in 2016. Building a permanent facility required significant funding, and the family continued looking for ways to support the work. Acho’s NFL career soon gave him an opportunity to contribute through charitable donations associated with his award nominations.
 Sam Acho’s two NFL award nominations brought $100,000 for the hospital
Acho played college football at the University of Texas before entering the NFL. The Arizona Cardinals selected him in the fourth round of the 2011 NFL Draft. He later played for the Chicago Bears and Tampa Bay Buccaneers while continuing to support his family’s charitable work.
His community involvement earned him two nominations for the Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year Award. The award recognises players for their work off the field alongside their achievements in football. Acho was the Chicago Bears’ nominee in both 2016 and 2017.
Each nomination came with a $50,000 charitable donation. Acho directed both donations to Living Hope Christian Ministries, bringing the total to $100,000 for the hospital project.
The first donation arrived just months after the family had decided to move ahead with construction. Acho recalled his reaction when he learned that the money could go directly toward the project.
“When did I get nominated for this award?” Acho recalled asking. “It was just months after we said ‘Let’s build.’ So that $50,000 went straight to Living Hope Christian Ministries, which went straight to the hospital.”
His second nomination in 2017 brought another $50,000 donation. Together, the two contributions gave the family $100,000 to help move the hospital project forward.
The money was part of a wider fundraising effort rather than the only source of support. Acho and his family also received help from people in the football community and supporters connected to the University of Texas. Fundraising events, including a celebrity waiter event that raised $60,000 in 2016, also helped the project.
The Living Hope Medical Center opened in June 2017. The facility gave patients a permanent place to seek medical care and helped the family move beyond the limits of its annual medical missions. Instead of relying only on visiting teams, the community now had access to a medical center throughout the year.
The opening marked a major step for a project that had grown out of the family’s work since 1989. Acho’s parents had spent years providing care during short visits, and the hospital offered a way to continue that service after volunteers returned home.
Reflecting on what the project had achieved, Acho said, “It’s just been amazing to see.” He also spoke about how one person’s belief and action could make a difference beyond their immediate community.
In Acho’s case, the hospital was a way to support a mission his parents had started long before his NFL career. His two award nominations brought $100,000 in charitable donations toward the facility, while years of medical missions and wider fundraising helped make the project possible.
The Living Hope Medical Center gave the family’s work a permanent base in Nigeria. What began as an effort to provide free treatment during annual visits eventually grew into a healthcare facility serving patients throughout the year.

briefs.headline: Shadab, Rauf pull off miracle with record 89-run stand for last wicket as PAK stun ENG
briefs.deck: Shadab Khan, who came in at number eight, did the unthinkable, stitching together an unbeaten 89-run partnership for the last wicket with Rauf to take Pakistan home in the fourth ODI of the tri-series, which also features Sri Lanka.
briefs.bodyText:
The game looked set for England when Haris Rauf walked out to bat at number 11 with Pakistan at 154 for 9 in their chase of 242, still needing 88 runs to win.
It looked like it was all over, and England certainly thought so. But Shadab Khan, who came in at number eight, did the unthinkable, stitching together an unbeaten 89-run partnership for the last wicket with Rauf to take Pakistan home in Lahore on Sunday. in the fourth ODI of the tri-series, which also features Sri Lanka.
Shadab chipped away at the target, finding a boundary in almost every over while managing to keep the strike with himself most of the time. Rauf played his part too, defending when needed and ducking and weaving as England threw everything at him. He hung in there to finish unbeaten on seven, while Shadab dictated terms at the other end. Rauf eventually hit the winning runs and raced away with his arms raised.
The unbeaten 89-run stand between Shadab and Rauf is now the highest for the 10th wicket in a successful ODI chase. The previous record was an unbeaten 64-run partnership between Deryck Murray and Andy Roberts against Pakistan at the 1975 World Cup.
Shadab scored his maiden ODI century, making 113 off 96 balls in a match-winning effort that turned the game on its head as England let victory slip away.
The win took Pakistan into the tri-series final.
England had made a strong start while defending their target, with their bowlers working together to prevent Pakistan from building partnerships. Pakistan lost their top three batters — Fakhar Zaman (10 off 18), Saim Ayub (6 off 12) and Babar Azam (10 off 12) — inside the powerplay. England continued to take wickets and reduced the hosts to 154 for 9, but could not get the final breakthrough as Shadab and Rauf guided Pakistan to a memorable win in Lahore.
Earlier, Pakistan captain and fast bowler Shaheen Shah Afridi took four wickets to restrict England to 241, despite a fighting century from Ben Duckett.
England, who needed a win to stay in contention for the tri-series after losing their first two matches, struggled to recover after slipping to 19 for 3 on a batting-friendly pitch.
Duckett scored 105 off 111 balls, while Sam Curran made 42 during a 93-run stand for the fifth wicket. Gus Atkinson added an unbeaten 36 towards the end of the innings.
Shaheen finished with figures of 4 for 46, while ODI debutant Razaullah took 2 for 38 as England were bowled out in 46.4 overs.

briefs.headline: Fasalul and his love for overcoming hurdles
briefs.bodyText:
A false start, a steady drizzle coupled with a mild breeze and cool conditions. And if that wasn’t enough, Keralam’s C.K. Fasalul Haque fell behind midway through the race before recovering to claim gold in the under-20 men’s 110m hurdles at the 41st National junior athletics championships at the Nehru Stadium here on Sunday.
The clock read 13.70 seconds, but it wasn’t quite the timing he had hoped for.
Fasalul knows what it takes to set a record, having clocked 13.61s in Pune in June to establish a new national under-20 mark. And despite winning gold, there was a hint of disappointment, for he had come hoping to better his own record.
“I was expecting to clock 13.40. I got a good lead, but in between, I hit a hurdle. I don’t know what happened after that,” Fasalul told The Hindu.
The weather, too, had a bearing on his performance.
“In Pune, the conditions were nice. I had a good warm-up and my body was warm. Today, I was feeling cold and couldn’t warm up properly,” said the 18-year-old.
Hailing from Malappuram, Fasalul took up athletics at the age of 15, starting with the 100m before his first coach encouraged him to try his hand at hurdles.
The transition to the higher hurdles in the u-20 category initially proved challenging, but Fasalul said he became comfortable with the height after a couple of months.
Unlike the 100m, where a poor start can prove costly, Fasalul believes the hurdles offer him an opportunity to recover lost ground.
“I don’t usually get good starts. I start pushing after the fifth or sixth hurdle. Even today, I was behind around 50 to 60 metres, but I managed to come back”, he said.
For now, the youngster has his sights set on another mark, this time at the senior level.
“I want to run below 13 seconds at the senior level and become the first Indian to do it. I’m 100 per cent sure I can”, he said.

briefs.headline: India dominate Zimbabwe as Harmanpreet, Deepti and Vaishnavi headline 121-run win
briefs.deck: In a dominant performance, India Women triumphed over Zimbabwe in the second ODI match, with both Harmanpreet Kaur and Deepti Sharma shining through with impressive centuries. Pratika Rawal added stability with a crucial innings, helping set a significant total. Zimbabwe struggled to chase, losing wickets consistently, ultimately bowled out for 207 and handing India a resounding 121-run victory.
briefs.bodyText:
India Women produced a commanding all-round performance to seal the three-match ODI series against Zimbabwe with a game to spare, registering a 121-run victory in the second ODI at the BCA Stadium in Vadodara on Sunday. Twin centuries from 
Harmanpreet Kaur
 and 
Deepti Sharma
 powered the hosts to a mammoth 328/6 before the bowlers dismantled Zimbabwe for 207 in 48.5 overs to secure an unassailable 2-0 lead.
Harmanpreet, Deepti power India to imposing total
India suffered an early setback when skipper Smriti Mandhana fell for a duck, but Pratika Rawal steadied the innings with a composed 61 off 67 balls. She shared a 124-run partnership for the third wicket with Harmanpreet, laying the foundation for a big total.
Harmanpreet took charge with a fluent 126 off 121 deliveries, striking 15 boundaries, while Deepti provided the late impetus with an unbeaten 106 off 86 balls. Deepti reached her century in just 83 deliveries, producing an aggressive counter-attacking knock that kept Zimbabwe's bowlers under pressure.
The pair added 153 runs off 138 balls for the fifth wicket, setting a new record for India's highest partnership for that wicket in women's ODIs. Their efforts lifted the hosts to 328/6 in 50 overs, leaving Zimbabwe with a daunting target of 329.
Nomvelo Sibanda was Zimbabwe's most successful bowler, claiming two wickets, but the visitors struggled to contain India's batters through the middle overs.
Vaishnavi, Deepti lead India's bowling charge
Zimbabwe showed greater resistance in the chase than they had in the opening match, with Modester Mupachikwa and Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano putting together a 69-run partnership to give the visitors some hope.
Mupachikwa made 49 off 70 balls, while Mugeri-Tiripano scored 46, but both fell in the 40s as India broke the partnership at a crucial stage. Zimbabwe were forced to rebuild, and the wickets continued to tumble as the required run rate climbed.
Vaishnavi, who returned to the XI in place of Kranti Gaud, made a decisive impact in the middle and lower overs, finishing with figures of 4/39 in 10 overs. Her disciplined bowling prevented Zimbabwe from building further partnerships and gave India control of the contest.
Deepti capped a memorable outing with the ball as well, taking 3/32 in nine overs after her century earlier in the day. Jintimani Kalita then claimed the final wicket of Chiedza Dhururu for her maiden international wicket, bowling Zimbabwe out for 207 in 48.5 overs.
